lessons.title: 1.1 The IELTS Test: Academic vs General Training
lessons.html:
The IELTS Test: Academic vs General TrainingLesson note
🤔 Let's start with a question
Two people both say they're “taking IELTS,” yet one is applying to university and the other is applying to immigrate. Are they even taking the same test?

The IELTS Test: Academic vs General Training

In plain words

IELTS comes in two versions: Academic, required for university admission, and General Training, used for migration, work, or secondary education — both share Listening and Speaking, but differ in Reading and Writing.

Choosing the right version is like applying for the correct visa type — related processes, but submitting the wrong one to the wrong institution causes real, serious problems, however well you actually performed.

Key differences at a glance

SectionAcademicGeneral Training
Listening & SpeakingIdenticalIdentical
ReadingLonger academic passagesEveryday texts like notices and ads
Writing Task 1Describe a chart or diagramWrite a letter (formal or informal)
Typical useUniversity admissionImmigration, work, secondary study

Why this matters to you

Confirming which version your target institution or immigration authority actually requires — before you even book the test — is the single most important first step, since results from the wrong version simply are not accepted where you need them.

🧪 Try it yourself: Check which version applies to your own goal (university, migration, or work) and confirm this with the institution or authority requiring it.

🔑 Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Academic IELTS

The version required for university admission

General Training IELTS

The version used for migration, work, or secondary education

Study tip: Never assume which version you need — confirm directly with the specific institution or authority requiring your score, since taking the wrong one means retaking the entire exam.

lessons.title: 1.2 Understanding the Band Score System (0–9)
lessons.html:
Understanding the Band Score System (0–9)Lesson note
🤔 Let's start with a question
A university asks for “Band 6.5 overall.” Is that one single score, or several different scores combined into one number?

Understanding the Band Score System (0–9)

In plain words

IELTS is scored on a band scale from 0 to 9 for each of the four skills, which are then averaged into one overall band score.

The band system is like a report card with four separate subject grades that get averaged into one final GPA — your overall score reflects a balance across all four skills, not just your strongest one.

How the scoring works

ConceptExplanation
Four individual scoresListening, Reading, Writing, Speaking, each scored 0-9
Overall band scoreThe average of all four, rounded to the nearest 0.5
Band descriptorsEach band level has specific, defined criteria (e.g. Band 7 = “good user”)
No pass or failIELTS has no fixed pass/fail; institutions set their own required band

Why this matters to you

Understanding that your overall score is an average means a genuine weakness in one skill can pull your whole score down — this is exactly why balanced practice across all four skills matters more than only polishing your strongest one.

🧪 Try it yourself: Look up (or recall) what your specific target band score requirement is, and identify which of the four skills currently feels like your weakest.

🔑 Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Band score

A score from 0 to 9 measuring English proficiency in IELTS

Band descriptor

The specific, defined criteria describing what each band level represents

Study tip: Identify your weakest of the four skills honestly, and direct extra study time there — since your overall score is an average, your weakest skill has real, direct power to hold back your whole result.

lessons.title: 1.3 Test-Day Logistics & Smart Preparation
lessons.html:
Test-Day Logistics & Smart PreparationLesson note
🤔 Let's start with a question
You've studied for months. Would forgetting your ID, or arriving five minutes late, really be allowed to undo all of that preparation?

Test-Day Logistics & Smart Preparation

In plain words

Test-day logistics covers the practical preparation — documents, timing, permitted items — needed to make sure your actual English ability is what gets tested, not avoidable logistical mistakes.

Good logistics preparation is like double-checking your passport and tickets before an important flight — it has nothing to do with the destination itself, but getting it wrong can still stop your whole journey.

Smart preparation checklist

ItemWhy it matters
Valid ID matching registration exactlyMismatches can mean being refused entry
Arrive well before the start timeLate arrival can mean losing your place entirely
Know your exact test formatPaper-based or computer-based changes what you should practise
Bring only permitted itemsUnpermitted items like phones can cause serious problems

Why this matters to you

Every year, some capable candidates lose their test attempt entirely over an avoidable logistical mistake — a few minutes spent confirming these practical details in advance protects the months of genuine study effort behind it.

🧪 Try it yourself: Confirm your own test date, location, exact ID requirements, and format (paper or computer-based) well in advance of your actual exam.

🔑 Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Registration details

The exact information submitted when booking your test

Permitted items

The specific belongings allowed into the exam room

Study tip: Confirm every logistical detail — ID, location, arrival time, format — at least a week before your test, so nothing avoidable can disrupt months of genuine preparation.

lessons.title: 2.1 The Four Sections & Every Question Type
lessons.html:
The Four Sections & Every Question TypeLesson note
🤔 Let's start with a question
IELTS Listening isn't just “listen and answer.” How many genuinely different question formats are actually hidden inside that one section?

The Four Sections & Every Question Type

In plain words

This lesson maps out IELTS Listening's four sections and every distinct question type within them, from multiple choice to map labelling.

Listening's four sections are like four different chapters of a book, each with its own setting and style — a social conversation, a monologue, an academic discussion, and a lecture — each demanding a slightly different listening approach.

The four Listening sections

SectionTypical content
Section 1A conversation about a everyday situation, like a booking
Section 2A monologue about a general topic, like a facility tour
Section 3A conversation between multiple people, often academic
Section 4A monologue lecture on an academic subject

Why this matters to you

Recognising which section and question type you're facing instantly tells you which specific strategy to apply — prediction, mapping, or note completion — rather than approaching every question with the exact same generic method.

🧪 Try it yourself: Match each section in the table above to one skill you've studied earlier in this course that would help with it.

🔑 Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Section

One of the four distinct parts of the IELTS Listening test

Question type

A specific format of question, like multiple choice or map labelling

Study tip: Learn the general content and difficulty of each of the four Listening sections in advance — it removes surprises and lets you apply the right strategy immediately.

lessons.title: 2.2 Strategies: Prediction, Keywords & Distractor Traps
lessons.html:
Strategies: Prediction, Keywords & Distractor TrapsLesson note
🤔 Let's start with a question
You already know prediction and distractor-spotting as separate skills. How do you actually combine them into one smooth, real-time listening strategy?

Strategies: Prediction, Keywords & Distractor Traps

In plain words

This lesson combines prediction, keyword spotting, and recognising distractor traps into one unified, practical Listening strategy.

Combining these three skills is like a driver simultaneously checking mirrors, signalling, and watching the road — each skill alone is simple, but real listening requires using all three together, continuously and in real time.

The combined strategy in action

SkillHow it's used together
PredictionGuess the likely answer type before listening starts
KeywordsIdentify the specific words in the question to listen for
Distractor trapsRecognise similar-sounding wrong options and avoid them

Why this matters to you

High-scoring candidates rarely use just one of these skills in isolation — they run all three simultaneously and automatically, which is exactly the kind of integrated fluency that comes from deliberate, combined practice like this.

🧪 Try it yourself: Take one practice Listening question and explicitly write out your prediction, your chosen keywords, and one likely distractor trap, before listening.

🔑 Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Integrated strategy

Using multiple techniques together, automatically, rather than one at a time

Keyword

A specific, distinctive word used to guide focused listening

Study tip: Practise applying prediction, keywords, and distractor-awareness together on every single practice question — running them simultaneously, not separately, is what builds real exam-ready listening.

lessons.title: 2.3 Spelling, Numbers & Transferring Answers
lessons.html:
Spelling, Numbers & Transferring AnswersLesson note
🤔 Let's start with a question
You understood every single answer correctly while listening. Yet you still lost marks. How is that even possible?

Spelling, Numbers & Transferring Answers

In plain words

This lesson focuses on the final, often overlooked step: correctly spelling answers, writing numbers accurately, and properly transferring them onto your answer sheet.

This is like cooking a perfect meal, then spilling it while carrying it to the table — understanding the content correctly means nothing if the final answer isn't recorded accurately.

Common transfer mistakes

MistakeFix
Misspelling a correctly heard wordDouble-check spelling, especially for names
Writing digits incorrectlyReread numbers carefully before finalising
Exceeding the word limitRecount your answer against the stated limit
Leaving an answer sheet blank by mistakeAlways write something, even an educated guess

Why this matters to you

A correctly understood answer that is misspelled or incorrectly transferred is marked wrong exactly as if you'd misheard it entirely — this final, careful step is just as important as the listening itself.

🧪 Try it yourself: Take five answers you're confident you understood correctly from any practice test, and double-check each one for spelling, digits, and word limit.

🔑 Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Transfer

Copying your answers accurately onto the final answer sheet

Word limit

The maximum number of words allowed for a specific answer

Study tip: Always leave a few minutes to carefully check your spelling, numbers, and word limits before finishing — this final review step protects marks you've already genuinely earned.

lessons.title: 3.1 Skimming, Scanning & Time Management
lessons.html:
Skimming, Scanning & Time ManagementLesson note
🤔 Let's start with a question
You know skimming and scanning individually. But with a strict 60-minute clock running across three whole passages, how do you actually combine them under real pressure?

Skimming, Scanning & Time Management

In plain words

This lesson combines skimming, scanning, and overall time management into one practical strategy for completing all three Reading passages within the strict time limit.

Using these together under time pressure is like a chef managing several dishes cooking at once — each individual skill (skimming, scanning) is simple alone, but real exam pressure demands running them together, continuously, against the clock.

The combined Reading approach

StepTime guide
Skim the whole passage first1-2 minutes for the overall idea
Read the questionsIdentify what to scan for
Scan for each specific answerEfficiently, not rereading unnecessarily
Move on if stuckNever let one question consume disproportionate time

Why this matters to you

Reading is the section where strong understanding most often gets undermined by poor time management — combining skimming, scanning, and strict time discipline together is what actually allows you to complete all three passages fully.

🧪 Try it yourself: Complete one timed Reading passage using this exact combined approach, and note how much time each step actually took you.

🔑 Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Time discipline

Sticking to a planned time budget, even under pressure

Combined strategy

Using multiple techniques together as one smooth process

Study tip: Practise this combined skim-then-scan approach under a real clock regularly — it's the only way to build a genuinely reliable sense of pacing for the real exam.

lessons.title: 3.2 True / False / Not Given (and Yes / No / Not Given)
lessons.html:
True / False / Not Given (and Yes / No / Not Given)Lesson note
🤔 Let's start with a question
These two question types look almost identical on the page. Do you actually know, instantly, which one you're looking at and why it matters?

True / False / Not Given (and Yes / No / Not Given)

In plain words

This lesson reviews both True/False/Not Given (for facts) and Yes/No/Not Given (for opinions) together, since they share the same underlying three-way logic.

Both question types work like the same fact-checking tool used on two different kinds of documents — one checking a factual report, the other checking someone's stated opinions — but the checking process itself is identical.

Comparing the two versions

True/False/Not GivenYes/No/Not Given
TestsFacts and informationThe writer's opinions and claims
“Not Given” meansThe passage never states this either wayThe passage never states this either way
Common mistakeConfusing “False” with “Not Given”Confusing “No” with “Not Given”

Why this matters to you

The single most common error across both versions is the same: assuming something is False or No when the passage actually just never mentions it — mastering this one distinction improves accuracy across both question types at once.

🧪 Try it yourself: Write one True/False/Not Given statement and one Yes/No/Not Given statement about the same short passage, to practise applying both versions of the same logic.

🔑 Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Not Given

When a passage never states a specific point either way

Writer's opinion

What the author personally believes, tested by Yes/No/Not Given specifically

Study tip: Before answering False or No, always ask “does the passage state the OPPOSITE, or does it just never mention this?” — this one question resolves the most common error in both question types.

lessons.title: 3.3 Matching Headings, Completion & Multiple Choice
lessons.html:
Matching Headings, Completion & Multiple ChoiceLesson note
🤔 Let's start with a question
Three very different Reading question types, one passage, one clock. How do you switch between totally different strategies without losing time?

Matching Headings, Completion & Multiple Choice

In plain words

This lesson reviews three distinct Reading question types together — matching headings, completion tasks, and multiple choice — and how to recognise and switch between them efficiently.

Switching between these question types is like a mechanic swapping tools for different jobs on the same car — the underlying skill (careful, efficient reading) stays the same, but each tool is used slightly differently.

Quick-reference strategy summary

Question typeCore strategy
Matching headingsSkim each paragraph for its overall main idea
Completion (sentence/summary)Scan for exact wording and check grammar fit
Multiple choiceRead all options first, eliminate clearly wrong ones

Why this matters to you

A real IELTS Reading passage often mixes several of these question types together — instantly recognising which strategy each specific question calls for, without hesitation, is what separates efficient, confident test-takers from those who lose time reorienting themselves.

🧪 Try it yourself: Look at a practice Reading passage's question types and identify, for each one, which of the three strategies above applies.

🔑 Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Strategy switching

Moving smoothly between different techniques as question types change

Quick-reference

A short, memorable summary used for fast recall under pressure

Study tip: Before answering any Reading question, first identify exactly which type it is — this single habit tells you immediately which of your practised strategies to apply.

questions.question: Skimming means:
options: Reading quickly for the general idea

questions.question: "Not Given" means:

questions.explanation: Headings summarise the central idea of a paragraph, not a single detail.

questions.question: Academic Reading gives you:

questions.question: A good time strategy is to:
options: Answer easy questions first and not get stuck
questions.explanation: Secure the marks you can get quickly and return to harder items with remaining time.

questions.question: Academic Reading contains how many passages?
questions.explanation: Three passages with 40 questions in 60 minutes.

questions.question: Scanning is used to:
options: Find a specific word or fact quickly
questions.explanation: Scanning locates specific information fast once you know what to look for.

questions.question: Yes / No / Not Given questions test:
questions.explanation: Yes/No/Not Given is about the writer’s views; True/False/Not Given is about facts.

questions.question: For sentence-completion answers you should:
options: Copy words exactly from the passage within the word limit
questions.explanation: Use the exact words from the text and respect the word limit.

questions.question: If a statement is true in real life but the passage never mentions it, the answer is:
questions.explanation: Use only the passage, if it is not stated, it is Not Given.

lessons.title: 4.1 Task 1 Academic: Describing Graphs, Charts & Processes
lessons.html:
Task 1 Academic: Describing Graphs, Charts & ProcessesLesson note
🤔 Let's start with a question
Academic Task 1 could show you a graph, a chart, a table, or even a diagram of a process. Is one single strategy really flexible enough for all of them?

Task 1 Academic: Describing Graphs, Charts & Processes

In plain words

This lesson reviews the complete approach to Academic Writing Task 1: describing graphs, charts, tables, and process diagrams objectively and accurately.

Handling any Task 1 visual is like being a skilled reporter who can cover a sports match, a weather report, or a business update equally well — the specific content changes, but the same objective, structured reporting approach applies to all of them.

The universal Task 1 approach

StepApplies to
Paraphrase the question in your introductionEvery visual type
Write a clear overview of the main trend(s)Charts, graphs, tables
Describe specific data with figuresCharts, graphs, tables
Describe stages in sequence, using passive voiceProcess diagrams specifically

Why this matters to you

Academic Task 1 is worth exactly as much as Task 2 toward your Writing score, yet is often under-practised — having one flexible, universal approach ready for whichever visual type appears removes uncertainty on exam day.

🧪 Try it yourself: Pick any chart, table, or diagram you can find and write a full introduction and overview paragraph for it, using the universal approach above.

🔑 Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Universal approach

One flexible strategy adaptable across different visual types

Objective description

Describing facts and data without personal opinion

Study tip: Practise with a genuine variety of Task 1 visual types (not just your favourite one) so your universal approach feels equally natural whichever type actually appears in your real exam.

lessons.title: 4.2 Task 1 General: Formal & Informal Letters
lessons.html:
Task 1 General: Formal & Informal LettersLesson note
🤔 Let's start with a question
General Training Task 1 never shows you a single chart — instead, you write a letter. Does that completely change how you should prepare?

Task 1 General: Formal & Informal Letters

In plain words

This lesson covers General Training Task 1: writing a formal or informal letter in response to a given situation, rather than describing data.

Unlike Academic Task 1's objective data description, this task is more like real, everyday correspondence — writing to a landlord, a friend, or a company, with the tone matched carefully to exactly who you're addressing.

Choosing the right tone

SituationTone needed
Writing to a company or officialFormal (“Dear Sir/Madam,”)
Writing to a landlord or manager you don't know wellSemi-formal (“Dear Mr. Johnson,”)
Writing to a friend or family memberInformal (“Hi Grace,”)

Why this matters to you

Task Achievement here specifically requires matching your tone correctly to the situation described in the prompt — a letter to a company written in an overly casual tone (or vice versa) loses marks regardless of how well-organised the letter otherwise is.

🧪 Try it yourself: Take a letter situation (like complaining to a company about a faulty product) and write just the opening greeting and first sentence in the appropriately formal tone.

🔑 Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Formal tone

Serious, respectful language used for official or unfamiliar recipients

Informal tone

Relaxed, friendly language used for people you know well

Study tip: Before writing a single word, identify who you're writing to and choose your tone deliberately — this decision shapes every single sentence that follows.

lessons.title: 4.3 Task 2: Essay Structure & Building an Argument
lessons.html:
Task 2: Essay Structure & Building an ArgumentLesson note
🤔 Let's start with a question
You know the standard four-part essay structure. But how do you actually make sure a strong, coherent ARGUMENT flows through it, not just correctly-placed paragraphs?

Task 2: Essay Structure & Building an Argument

In plain words

This lesson reviews Task 2 essay structure alongside the skill of building a genuine argument that flows logically from introduction to conclusion.

Correct structure without a real argument is like a well-built house with no clear purpose inside it — the four-part shape must actually carry one consistent, developing line of reasoning, not just correctly-labelled sections.

Structure serving the argument

PartWhat the argument needs here
IntroductionState your clear position, which the whole essay will support
Body paragraphsEach one builds evidence directly supporting that same position
ConclusionConfirms the same position, now backed by everything just argued

Why this matters to you

A high-scoring essay isn't simply four correctly-shaped paragraphs — it's one consistent argument that a reader can follow clearly from the very first sentence to the very last, with every paragraph genuinely supporting the same stated position.

🧪 Try it yourself: Take an essay question and write just your introduction's position statement, then check that both your planned body paragraphs would genuinely support that exact same position.

🔑 Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Argument

A consistent line of reasoning supporting one clear position throughout

Consistent position

Maintaining the same stated view from introduction to conclusion

Study tip: Before writing your body paragraphs, reread your introduction's stated position — every paragraph that follows should visibly and directly support that exact same view.

lessons.title: 4.4 Cohesion, Vocabulary & Common Mistakes
lessons.html:
Cohesion, Vocabulary & Common MistakesLesson note
🤔 Let's start with a question
You've studied cohesion, vocabulary, and common mistakes separately. How do all three combine into one final, practical writing review checklist?

Cohesion, Vocabulary & Common Mistakes

In plain words

This lesson combines cohesion (how ideas connect), vocabulary range, and avoiding common mistakes into one practical final review process for any Task 2 essay.

Reviewing an essay this way is like a final quality check before shipping a product — checking connections, checking materials (vocabulary), and checking for known defects (common mistakes), all in one pass before calling it finished.

A combined final review checklist

CheckWhat to look for
CohesionDo linking words connect ideas smoothly and logically?
VocabularyIs there variety, or are the same simple words repeated too often?
Common mistakesAny memorised generic phrases, missing word count, or ignored question parts?

Why this matters to you

Running this three-part check as a final review, right before submitting any Task 2 essay, catches exactly the kind of small, avoidable issues that otherwise quietly cap an essay's score despite genuinely strong underlying ideas.

🧪 Try it yourself: Take any essay you've written and run it through all three checks in the table above, noting at least one specific improvement for each.

🔑 Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Final review

A last, deliberate check of a finished piece of writing before submitting it

Combined checklist

Several separate checks run together as one final process

Study tip: Always leave five minutes at the end of Task 2 for exactly this three-part review — it's often enough time to catch and fix several small, otherwise costly issues.

lessons.title: 🛠️ Project: Write a Full Band 7 Task 2 Essay

Project: Write a Full Band 7 Task 2 EssayLesson note

Project: Write a Full Band 7 Task 2 Essay

This final project asks you to write one complete Task 2 essay, applying every Writing skill from this course together — structure, argument, vocabulary, grammar range, and cohesion.

This project is like a final exam after a full term of separate lessons — not learning anything new, but proving you can bring every previously separate skill together into one finished, polished piece of work.

Applying everything together

Skill areaWhere it was covered
Essay structure & argumentTask 2 essay-type lessons
Vocabulary range & precisionAdvanced Vocabulary, Collocations

Completing one full, genuine essay under real timed conditions (250 words, 40 minutes) is the single most valuable final practice activity in this entire course — it's where every separately-studied skill either comes together successfully, or reveals exactly what still needs work.

Complete response

A full essay addressing every part of the task, from introduction to conclusion

Practising under the exact time limit of the real exam

lessons.title: 5.1 Part 1: Introduction & Interview
lessons.html:
Part 1: Introduction & InterviewLesson note
🤔 Let's start with a question
The Speaking test's opening minutes set the tone for everything that follows. Do you have a clear, confident plan for exactly how to handle them?

Part 1: Introduction & Interview

In plain words

This lesson reviews Speaking Part 1: the introduction and interview-style questions covering familiar, everyday topics about yourself.

Part 1 is like the friendly small talk at the start of a job interview — relatively low-pressure, but still your first real chance to make a strong, confident impression before the harder questions begin.

A confident Part 1 approach

ElementApproach
Opening greetingRespond naturally and confidently to the examiner's welcome
Familiar topic questionsExpand every answer with a reason or example
PacingKeep answers to a natural 20-30 seconds, not too short or too long

Why this matters to you

A strong, confident Part 1 sets a positive tone that can genuinely carry through the rest of your test — practising expanded, natural answers to the most common topics (home, work, family, hobbies) removes any early hesitation.

🧪 Try it yourself: Practise answering three typical Part 1 questions out loud, each expanded with a reason or example, keeping each answer to about 20-30 seconds.

🔑 Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Interview questions

Everyday, familiar questions asked directly by the examiner

Expanded answer

A response including a reason or example, not just a short phrase

Study tip: Prepare confident, expanded answers for the handful of near-certain Part 1 topics — home, family, work, studies, hobbies — so this opening section feels genuinely natural, not rehearsed.

lessons.title: 5.2 Part 2: The Long Turn (Cue Card)
lessons.html:
Part 2: The Long Turn (Cue Card)Lesson note
🤔 Let's start with a question
For two whole minutes, you speak alone with no questions from the examiner. Could you actually sustain that, confidently, right now?

Part 2: The Long Turn (Cue Card)

In plain words

This lesson reviews Speaking Part 2, the “long turn”: one minute to prepare using a cue card, then up to two minutes speaking alone on that topic.

Part 2 is like giving a short, unscripted presentation — you're handed a topic and a moment to prepare, then must speak fluently and confidently without any back-and-forth support from the examiner.

Making the most of Part 2

StepApproach
Use the full one-minute prep timeJot quick notes for every bullet point
Structure your answer around the bullet pointsEnsures full topic coverage
Add extra detail if you finish earlyKeep speaking naturally until time is called
Stay calm if the examiner stops youThis is normal; it does not mean you did poorly

Why this matters to you

Part 2 specifically tests your ability to speak at length, independently and fluently — using every bullet point as a mini-outline, then adding natural extra detail, is the most reliable way to sustain a full, confident two-minute answer.

🧪 Try it yourself: Pick a cue card topic, use one minute to prepare quick notes, then speak about it out loud for as close to two full minutes as you can.

🔑 Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Long turn

The extended, largely uninterrupted speaking portion of Part 2

Bullet point coverage

Addressing every point listed on the cue card

Study tip: Treat the cue card's bullet points as your outline, not a strict script — covering all of them while speaking naturally is what fills the full two minutes confidently.

lessons.title: 5.3 Part 3: Discussion, Fluency & Pronunciation
lessons.html:
Part 3: Discussion, Fluency & PronunciationLesson note
🤔 Let's start with a question
Part 3 asks broader, more abstract questions than Part 1 or 2. Does that also change what the examiner is specifically listening for in HOW you answer?

Part 3: Discussion, Fluency & Pronunciation

In plain words

This lesson reviews Speaking Part 3: a deeper discussion connected to your Part 2 topic, specifically testing sustained fluency and clear pronunciation on more abstract questions.

Part 3 is like moving from a friendly chat into a genuine discussion of ideas — the examiner is now listening closely for how confidently and clearly you can reason through more complex, less personal topics.

What Part 3 specifically rewards

FocusWhat strong performance looks like
Depth of reasoningExplaining WHY, not just giving a short opinion
Sustained fluencySpeaking smoothly across longer, more complex answers
Clear pronunciationRemaining easily understood even under more challenging questions
Balanced viewsAcknowledging other perspectives where genuinely relevant

Why this matters to you

Part 3 is often where higher-band candidates most clearly distinguish themselves — sustained fluency and clear pronunciation on genuinely challenging, abstract questions demonstrate a depth of English control that simpler Part 1 answers cannot fully reveal.

🧪 Try it yourself: Take a broader discussion question related to a topic you've practised before, and answer it out loud for a full minute, focusing on staying fluent and clear.

🔑 Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Sustained fluency

Maintaining smooth, natural speech across a longer, more demanding answer

Depth of reasoning

Explaining the “why” behind an opinion, not just stating it

Study tip: Practise explaining your reasoning at length on unfamiliar, broader topics — Part 3 specifically rewards depth and sustained fluency over short, simple opinions.

modules.title: Module 6: Vocabulary, Grammar & Your Band 7+ Plan

lessons.title: 6.1 Vocabulary for Band 7+: Collocations & Precision
lessons.html:
Vocabulary for Band 7+: Collocations & PrecisionLesson note
🤔 Let's start with a question
You know plenty of individual advanced words. But do you know which ones naturally belong together, the way a native speaker instinctively would?

Vocabulary for Band 7+: Collocations & Precision

In plain words

This lesson focuses on collocations (words that naturally pair together) and using vocabulary with genuine precision, both essential for Band 7+ Lexical Resource.

Precise collocations are like knowing which specific ingredients traditionally pair together in a recipe — technically you could substitute something similar, but the natural pairing is what experienced cooks (or speakers) instinctively reach for.

Building precise, natural vocabulary

Weak/impreciseBand 7+ collocation
“do a mistake”“make a mistake”
“very important”“crucial” or “of paramount importance”
“big problem”“significant issue” or “pressing concern”

Why this matters to you

At Band 7+, examiners specifically listen and read for natural word pairings and precise vocabulary choices, not just impressive-sounding individual words — collocation accuracy is often what separates a genuinely high score from a merely good one.

🧪 Try it yourself: Take three simple phrases you commonly use and upgrade each one to a more natural, precise collocation using the table above as a model.

🔑 Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Collocation

Words that naturally pair together in a language

Precision

Choosing the exact right word for a specific meaning, not just a similar one

Study tip: Learn new vocabulary in full collocation phrases, not single words — memorising “make a mistake” as one unit avoids the common, natural-sounding errors many advanced learners still make.

lessons.title: 6.2 Grammar Range: Complex Sentences Without Errors
lessons.html:
Grammar Range: Complex Sentences Without ErrorsLesson note
🤔 Let's start with a question
You can write complex sentences using “although” and “which.” But does adding that complexity accidentally introduce new grammar mistakes?

Grammar Range: Complex Sentences Without Errors

In plain words

This lesson focuses on using genuinely complex sentence structures while maintaining full grammatical accuracy — the real Band 7+ combination.

This is like a driver learning to handle a more powerful car — genuine skill isn't just going faster (more complexity), but maintaining full control and accuracy while doing so.

Balancing complexity and accuracy

ApproachResult
Only simple sentencesAccurate, but capped Grammatical Range score
Complex sentences with frequent errorsShows range attempted, but errors still cap the score
Complex sentences used correctlyThe genuine Band 7+ combination

Why this matters to you

Grammatical Range and Accuracy specifically rewards BOTH range and correctness together — attempting complex structures you're not fully confident with, and getting them wrong repeatedly, can actually score worse than using fewer, but fully accurate, complex sentences.

🧪 Try it yourself: Write three complex sentences using different structures (“although,” “which,” “as a result of”), and check each one carefully for grammatical accuracy.

🔑 Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Grammatical Range and Accuracy

The IELTS scoring criterion rewarding both sentence variety and correctness

Full control

Using a structure confidently and correctly, not just attempting it

Study tip: Only use a complex structure in your real exam if you're genuinely confident using it correctly — a smaller number of accurate complex sentences scores better than many attempted but error-filled ones.

lessons.title: 6.3 The Full Mock Test: Practice Under Real Exam Conditions
lessons.html:
The Full Mock Test: Practice Under Real Exam ConditionsLesson note
🤔 Let's start with a question
You've studied every skill and strategy in this course. Is there really anything left to learn from sitting one final, complete practice test?

The Full Mock Test: Practice Under Real Exam Conditions

In plain words

A full mock test means completing an entire, timed IELTS exam — all four skills, in order, under strict real exam conditions — as the ultimate rehearsal before test day.

This final mock test is like a full dress rehearsal the night before a real performance — every individual skill has already been trained separately, but this is where you confirm they all genuinely work together, under real pressure.

Getting the most from your mock test

StepWhy it matters
Complete all four sections in one sittingBuilds genuine stamina for the real exam's full length
Follow the real timing exactlyNo pausing, no extra time
Simulate real conditionsQuiet space, no dictionary, no interruptions
Review honestly afterwardIdentify your true current weak points before the real exam

Why this matters to you

This final mock test is the single best final rehearsal available before the real exam — it reveals problems (like fatigue by the last section, or timing slips across a full sitting) that no amount of isolated skill practice alone can show you.

🧪 Try it yourself: Schedule and complete one full, strictly timed mock test covering all four skills, then honestly review your results afterward.

🔑 Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Full mock test

A complete, timed practice exam covering all four skills at once

Honest review

Assessing your results accurately, without minimising real weaknesses

Study tip: Treat your final mock test exactly like the real exam — strict timing, real conditions, honest scoring — since this realistic rehearsal builds the most reliable, transferable exam-day confidence.

lessons.title: 6.4 Your 30-Day Study Plan & Test-Week Checklist
lessons.html:
Your 30-Day Study Plan & Test-Week ChecklistLesson note
🤔 Let's start with a question
You know everything this course has covered. But with 30 days until your real exam, do you actually have a clear day-by-day plan for using that time well?

Your 30-Day Study Plan & Test-Week Checklist

In plain words

This final lesson helps you build a practical 30-day study plan and a test-week checklist, turning everything learned in this course into one clear, actionable schedule.

A 30-day plan is like a training schedule before a big race — rather than randomly practising whatever feels interesting each day, a clear plan ensures every skill area gets deliberate, balanced attention before the real test.

Building your 30-day plan

Time frameFocus
Days 1-10Review weakest skills identified through error analysis
Days 11-20Full timed practice sections, one skill area per day
Days 21-27One or two full mock tests, with honest review
Days 28-30 (test week)Light review only; confirm logistics; rest well

Why this matters to you

Cramming intensely right up until test day tends to increase anxiety and reduce performance — a structured plan that tapers into lighter review during test week, combined with confirming all logistics early, is what actually supports peak performance on the real day.

🧪 Try it yourself: Sketch your own personal 30-day plan (or a version scaled to however much time you actually have left) using the four phases in the table above.

🔑 Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Study plan

A structured schedule of what to practise and when, leading up to a test

Tapering

Gradually reducing intensity as test day approaches, to arrive rested and confident

Study tip: Build your own realistic study plan today, however much time you actually have left — a clear, balanced plan beats random, last-minute cramming every time.

questions.question: What does the examiner reward most under "Lexical Resource" at Band 7?
options: Flexible, precise vocabulary with natural collocations
questions.explanation: Band 7 rewards flexibility and precision, using less common items and collocations naturally, not memorized "big words".

questions.question: Which of these is a natural English collocation?
questions.explanation: "Heavy rain" is a natural collocation. Collocations are word partners that native speakers use together.

questions.question: A complex sentence contains…
options: At least one independent clause and one dependent clause
questions.explanation: A complex sentence joins an independent clause with a dependent clause (e.g. using although, because, which).

questions.question: Using memorized "fancy" phrases that do not fit the question will…
options: Lower your score, examiners recognize memorized language
questions.explanation: Examiners are trained to spot memorized language and mark it down when it does not answer the question naturally.

questions.question: The most useful way to take a full mock test is…
options: One sitting, strictly timed, no dictionary, then review every mistake
questions.explanation: Simulating real conditions builds stamina and timing; the error review afterwards is where the learning happens.

questions.question: For Grammatical Range & Accuracy at Band 7, you need…
options: A variety of complex structures with most sentences error-free
Only simple sentences with no errors
questions.explanation: Band 7 requires a mix of structures where the majority of sentences are error-free, variety plus control.

questions.question: A good 30-day study plan should…
options: Focus only on your strongest skill
Cover all four skills with regular timed practice and error review
Leave writing until the last day
Avoid mock tests to reduce stress
questions.explanation: Balanced daily work across Listening, Reading, Writing and Speaking, with timed practice and review, moves your band fastest.

questions.question: In the final week before your test you should…
options: Stay up late practising every night
Do light review, one timed practice, and protect your sleep
questions.explanation: The last week is for consolidation and rest, cramming new material or losing sleep hurts performance on test day.

lessons.title: 1.1 English Alphabet & Pronunciation
lessons.html:
English Alphabet & PronunciationLesson note
🤔 Let's start with a question
You can read every letter of the alphabet perfectly, yet still say a word wrong out loud. Why does that happen with English?

English Alphabet & Pronunciation

In plain words

Pronunciation means saying the sounds of English clearly and correctly, so people understand you the first time, without asking you to repeat yourself.

English is tricky because letters don't always make the sound you'd expect — think of it like a road sign that sometimes points a different way than the road actually goes, so you have to learn the real route, not just the sign.

The building blocks of pronunciation

PartWhat it means
26 letters5 vowels (a, e, i, o, u) and 21 consonants
Letter name vs. sound“C” is named “see” but sounds like “k” in cat
StressWhich part of a word you say louder/longer, like PHO-to-graph
Spelling aloudSaying each letter clearly, useful for names and addresses

Why this matters to you

In the real IELTS Listening test, names and words are often spelled out loud, and clear pronunciation directly affects your Speaking score — examiners must understand you easily to give you a high mark.

🧪 Try it yourself: Say your own full name out loud, letter by letter, as if spelling it for a stranger over the phone. Record yourself if you can, and listen back.

🔑 Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Pronunciation

Saying the sounds of a language clearly and correctly

Vowel

One of the letters a, e, i, o, u

Stress

The extra emphasis given to one syllable in a word

Study tip: Practise spelling your own name and address out loud regularly — it's a skill tested directly in real IELTS Listening sections.

lessons.title: 2.1 Basic Grammar
lessons.html:
Basic GrammarLesson note
🤔 Let's start with a question
“She go to market” and “She goes to market” — only one is correct. Does that one small letter really matter that much?

Basic Grammar

In plain words

Grammar is the set of rules for arranging words correctly, so your sentences make clear, accurate sense to anyone listening or reading.

Grammar is like the frame of a house: the bricks (words) can be beautiful, but if the frame is wrong, the whole structure feels unstable and hard to trust.

Core grammar rules to know first

RuleExample
Subject-verb agreement“She walks”, not “She walk”
TensesPast (walked), present (walk), future (will walk)
ArticlesUse “a”, “an”, and “the” correctly before nouns
Word orderSubject + verb + object: “I eat rice”, not “Rice I eat”

Why this matters to you

Both IELTS Writing and Speaking are directly scored on grammatical range and accuracy — even simple, correct sentences earn real marks, while repeated errors quietly cap your band score no matter how good your ideas are.

🧪 Try it yourself: Take three sentences you'd normally say about your day and check each one against the four rules in the table above.

🔑 Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Grammar

The rules for how words are correctly arranged in a language

Tense

The form of a verb showing when an action happens (past, present, future)

Article

The words “a”, “an”, and “the”, used before nouns

Study tip: Even simple, grammatically correct sentences score better than ambitious ones full of errors — accuracy beats complexity at this stage.

lessons.title: 3.1 Parts of Speech
lessons.html:
Parts of SpeechLesson note
🤔 Let's start with a question
Every single word in a sentence has a specific “job.” Do you know what job each word in this very sentence is doing?

Parts of Speech

In plain words

Parts of speech are the categories every word falls into — noun, verb, adjective, adverb, pronoun — based on the job it does in a sentence.

Think of a sentence like a small team: the noun is the player carrying the ball, the verb is the action they take, and the adjective is the commentary describing how well they're doing it.

The main parts of speech

TypeJobExample
NounNames a person, place, or thingteacher, Monrovia, book
VerbShows an action or staterun, eat, is
AdjectiveDescribes a nountall, happy, blue
AdverbDescribes a verbquickly, well, often
PronounReplaces a nounhe, she, it, they

Why this matters to you

Recognising parts of speech helps you build accurate sentences in Writing, choose the right word forms in Speaking, and follow complicated sentence structures more easily in Reading passages.

🧪 Try it yourself: Take the sentence “The kind woman sells fresh fish quickly” and label each word's part of speech using the table above.

🔑 Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Noun

A word naming a person, place, or thing

Verb

A word showing an action or state

Adjective

A word describing a noun

Study tip: When a sentence feels confusing, try labelling each word's part of speech — it often reveals exactly where the structure breaks down.

lessons.title: 4.1 Common Vocabulary
lessons.html:
Common VocabularyLesson note
🤔 Let's start with a question
You know English grammar rules perfectly, but if you're missing the actual words, can you really say anything at all?

Common Vocabulary

In plain words

Vocabulary is the stock of words you know and can use confidently — covering everyday topics like home, food, work, school, and travel.

Vocabulary is like bricks for building a house: grammar is the blueprint for how to arrange them, but without enough bricks, there's no house to build at all, however good the blueprint is.

Everyday vocabulary categories

CategoryExamples
Everyday nounsmarket, home, road, money, phone
Common verbsgo, buy, work, help, learn
Useful adjectivesbig, small, cheap, busy, kind

Why this matters to you

A wider vocabulary raises your score across all four IELTS skills: in Speaking and Writing you express ideas more precisely, and in Listening and Reading you simply recognise and understand more of what you hear and read.

🧪 Try it yourself: Describe your typical day out loud in three or four sentences, using at least five words from the categories above.

🔑 Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Vocabulary

The words a person knows and can use

Learn in groups

Studying related words together by topic, to remember them faster

Study tip: Learn new words in topic groups (like “market words” or “travel words”) rather than as one long, random list — it sticks far better in memory.

lessons.title: 5.1 Sentence Structure
lessons.html:
Sentence StructureLesson note
🤔 Let's start with a question
You know plenty of English words. But if you just throw them together in any order, will anyone actually understand you?

Sentence Structure

In plain words

Sentence structure is the correct order of words that turns a pile of vocabulary into one clear, complete thought.

A sentence without proper structure is like ingredients dumped in a bowl without a recipe — everything needed might be there, but it doesn't come together into something anyone can actually use.

The basic sentence pattern

PartQuestion it answersExample
SubjectWho or what?My sister
VerbWhat action?sells
ObjectWho/what receives the action?vegetables

Why this matters to you

Clear sentence structure in IELTS Writing makes your ideas immediately understandable to the examiner, and in Speaking it helps you sound organised and confident rather than hesitant or jumbled.

🧪 Try it yourself: Build three complete sentences about your own life, each clearly following the subject + verb + object pattern.

🔑 Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Subject

Who or what a sentence is about

Object

Who or what receives the action in a sentence

Complete sentence

A sentence expressing one full, clear idea

Study tip: Master the basic subject + verb + object pattern first — every longer, more complex sentence you'll build later still relies on getting this right.

lessons.title: 6.1 Daily Conversations
lessons.html:
Daily ConversationsLesson note
🤔 Let's start with a question
Real English isn't just found in textbooks — it's in the small, quick chats you have every single day. How comfortable are you with those?

Daily Conversations

In plain words

Daily conversations are the short, everyday exchanges — greeting someone, asking a price, chatting about the weather — that build genuine speaking confidence.

Daily conversations are like warm-up exercises before a big match: small and simple on their own, but they build exactly the comfort and reflexes you need for the real performance later.

Building blocks of a daily conversation

ElementExample
Opener“How are you?”, “How is the family?”
Everyday topicfood, weather, work, plans
Polite wordsplease, thank you, sorry, excuse me
Turn-takinglisten fully, then respond

Why this matters to you

The IELTS Speaking test is designed to feel like a natural, friendly conversation — the more you practise real daily talk, the more relaxed and fluent you'll sound when the actual exam conversation begins.

🧪 Try it yourself: Have a short, real conversation today (in person or by phone) entirely in English, even just five exchanges, and notice which parts felt easy or hard.

🔑 Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Opener

A phrase used to start a conversation

Turn-taking

Listening, then responding, in a back-and-forth conversation

Study tip: Practising short, real conversations regularly builds far more speaking confidence than only studying grammar rules silently.

lessons.title: 7.1 Greetings & Introductions
lessons.html:
Greetings & IntroductionsLesson note
🤔 Let's start with a question
You meet someone new for the first time. What you say in the very first ten seconds — does it actually matter that much?

Greetings & Introductions

In plain words

Greetings are the words used to say hello, and introductions are how you tell someone who you are, both shaping a person's very first impression of you.

A warm greeting and clear introduction are like a firm, friendly handshake — a small gesture that sets the whole tone for everything that follows in the conversation.

Greeting and introducing yourself

SituationWhat to say
Greeting“Good morning”, “Hello”, “Good evening”
Introducing yourself“My name is...”, “I am from...”
Introducing someone else“This is my friend, Grace.”
Responding“Nice to meet you”, “Pleased to meet you.”

Why this matters to you

The IELTS Speaking test always begins with the examiner greeting you and asking about yourself — a confident, natural greeting and introduction sets a calm, positive tone for your entire test from the very first exchange.

🧪 Try it yourself: Practise introducing yourself out loud exactly as you would to an IELTS examiner: your name, where you're from, and one short extra detail.

🔑 Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Greeting

A polite word or phrase used to say hello

Introduction

Telling someone who you are

Study tip: Practise your self-introduction until it feels completely natural — it's very likely the first thing you'll say in your real IELTS Speaking test.

lessons.title: 8.1 Numbers, Dates & Time
lessons.html:
Numbers, Dates & TimeLesson note
🤔 Let's start with a question
An appointment is set for “half past nine on the 12th.” If you mishear even one of those numbers, what happens?

Numbers, Dates & Time

In plain words

This topic covers correctly saying and understanding numbers, calendar dates, and the time of day — details used constantly in prices, ages, and appointments.

Numbers and dates are like the exact coordinates on a map: being close isn't good enough — “around nine-ish” instead of “half past nine” can genuinely mean showing up at the wrong moment entirely.

Key patterns to know

CategoryExample
Numbersone, two, twenty, one hundred; prices like 250
Dates“the 12th of August” or “August 12th”
Time“half past seven”, “quarter to nine”, “eight o'clock”
Days/monthsMonday–Sunday, January–December

Why this matters to you

IELTS Listening frequently tests numbers, dates, and times inside bookings, forms, and phone messages — catching these correctly is some of the easiest scoring in the entire test, and the same skill helps constantly in real jobs and travel.

🧪 Try it yourself: Say your own date of birth, and the current time, fully out loud in English, using the patterns from the table above.

🔑 Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Date

A specific day, given as a day, month, and sometimes year

Time

The specific hour and minute, like “half past seven”

Study tip: Numbers, dates, and times appear constantly in Listening Section 1 — mastering them is one of the fastest ways to secure guaranteed marks.

lessons.title: 9.1 Family & Friends
lessons.html:
Family & FriendsLesson note
🤔 Let's start with a question
An examiner asks, “Tell me about your family.” Could you answer comfortably, right now, for a full thirty seconds?

Family & Friends

In plain words

This topic covers the vocabulary for describing family members and friends, one of the most common and comfortable subjects in everyday English conversation.

Family and friends are like your “home turf” topic — since you already know these people better than almost any other subject, this should be one of the easiest topics to speak about fluently and confidently.

Vocabulary for family and friends

CategoryExamples
Family wordsmother, father, brother, sister, aunt, uncle, cousin
Relationships“She is my older sister.”
Friendsbest friend, neighbour, classmate
Describing themkind, funny, hardworking, helpful

Why this matters to you

Family and friends are among the most frequent topics in IELTS Speaking Part 1 — being fully ready to describe the real people in your life lets you answer smoothly, naturally, and with genuine, specific detail.

🧪 Try it yourself: Describe one family member and one friend out loud, in two or three sentences each, using words from the table above.

🔑 Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Relationship

How one person is connected to another, like sister or neighbour

Describing word

An adjective used to describe a person's character, like kind or hardworking

Study tip: Prepare a few genuine, specific details about your real family and friends in advance — specific detail always sounds more natural and confident than vague, generic answers.

lessons.title: 10.1 Describing People
lessons.html:
Describing PeopleLesson note
🤔 Let's start with a question
“He is nice” — technically true, but does it actually help someone picture who you mean?

Describing People

In plain words

Describing people means using specific words to talk about both someone's appearance (how they look) and their personality (what kind of character they have).

A vague description is like a blurry photo — “nice” could mean almost anyone, while “patient and always smiling” lets the listener actually picture a real, specific person in their mind.

Describing appearance and personality

CategoryExamples
Appearancetall, short, slim, dark hair, kind face
Ageyoung, old, middle-aged, in her thirties
Personalityfriendly, patient, hardworking, honest

Why this matters to you

In IELTS Speaking Part 2 you may be asked to describe a person you admire — knowing specific describing words lets you speak confidently for the full two minutes with real, memorable detail, instead of running out of things to say after ten seconds.

🧪 Try it yourself: Describe a teacher, mentor, or person you admire out loud for thirty seconds, combining both appearance and personality details.

🔑 Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Appearance

How someone looks physically

Personality

The kind of character a person has

Study tip: Prepare specific, combined appearance + personality descriptions of two or three real people in advance — it makes Part 2 answers far easier to sustain for the full two minutes.

lessons.title: 1.1 Listening for Names and Numbers
lessons.html:
Listening for Names and NumbersLesson note
🤔 Let's start with a question
Someone says their name and phone number quickly on a recording. Do you catch every single letter and digit correctly the first time?

Listening for Names and Numbers

In plain words

This skill is about hearing names and numbers accurately, even when they are spoken quickly, spelled out, or corrected mid-sentence.

Listening for names and numbers is like catching small, fast-moving objects — you can't rewind real life, so you train yourself to grab the exact detail the instant it passes by.

A step-by-step approach

  1. Read the question first, so you already know what detail to expect.
  2. Listen for spelling; write each letter down as you hear it.
  3. For numbers, write the digits quickly, then double check them.
  4. Watch for corrections, like “sorry, that is 7, not 8.”
  5. Review your final answer for correct spelling and complete numbers.

Why this matters to you

This exact skill is tested heavily in IELTS Listening Section 1, where forms and bookings are full of spelled names and phone numbers — these are some of the easiest, most guaranteed marks in the whole test if you listen carefully.

🧪 Try it yourself: Ask someone to say a made-up name (spelled out) and a phone number out loud at a normal pace, and try writing both down correctly on the first listen.

🔑 Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Spelling out

Saying a word letter by letter, so it is understood exactly

Correction

When a speaker fixes something they just said, like a wrong number

Study tip: Always listen for corrections until the very end of a sentence — the speaker's final number or spelling is the one that counts, not the first one mentioned.

lessons.title: 2.1 Listening for Directions
lessons.html:
Listening for DirectionsLesson note
🤔 Let's start with a question
A recording explains how to get from the train station to a hotel. Could you actually follow that route just from listening, with no map?

Listening for Directions

In plain words

This skill involves understanding spoken directions — turns, distances, and landmarks — well enough to picture and follow a route just from listening.

Listening for directions is like following a friend's voice instructions while blindfolded — you must build an accurate mental map purely from what you hear, in the exact order it's given.

Key direction language

PhraseMeaning
Turn left/rightChange direction at a specific point
Go straight onContinue in the same direction
Next to / opposite / behindPosition relative to a landmark
At the end of / on the corner ofA specific location marker

Why this matters to you

IELTS Listening often includes a map-based question where you must trace a route or mark a location as it's described — recognising direction language quickly is essential to answering these questions accurately.

🧪 Try it yourself: Ask someone to describe, out loud, the route from your home to a nearby, familiar place, and try picturing or sketching it as they speak.

🔑 Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Landmark

A noticeable place or building used to give directions

Route

The path taken from one place to another

Study tip: As you listen to directions, try sketching a simple line for the route — turning information into a picture makes it much easier to follow and remember.

lessons.title: 3.1 Everyday Conversations
lessons.html:
Everyday ConversationsLesson note
🤔 Let's start with a question
Two friends chat about weekend plans in a recording. Can you follow not just the words, but who actually agrees with whom?

Everyday Conversations

In plain words

This skill focuses on understanding natural, everyday conversations between two or more people, including their opinions, agreements, and disagreements.

Following a natural conversation while listening is like watching a tennis match — you must track who is speaking, what point they're making, and how the other person responds, all while it moves quickly.

What to listen for

ElementWhy it matters
Who is speakingAnswers may depend on which speaker said what
Agreement/disagreementPhrases like “I think so too” or “Actually, I disagree”
Changes of planConversations often shift partway through
ToneCan reveal whether someone is excited, unsure, or annoyed

Why this matters to you

Real IELTS Listening sections include conversations between two speakers discussing plans or opinions — correctly tracking who says what, and how their views change, is essential to answering accurately.

🧪 Try it yourself: Listen to (or imagine) two people planning something together, and note down at least one point where they agree and one where they disagree.

🔑 Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Agreement

When speakers share the same opinion

Disagreement

When speakers hold different opinions

Study tip: Pay close attention whenever you hear words like “actually” or “but” — they often signal a change of plan or a disagreement about to follow.

lessons.title: 4.1 Understanding Simple Instructions
lessons.html:
Understanding Simple InstructionsLesson note
🤔 Let's start with a question
A recording tells you exactly how to fill out a form, step by step. If you miss step 2, does step 3 still make sense?

Understanding Simple Instructions

In plain words

This skill means following spoken instructions given in a specific order, understanding exactly what to do at each step.

Instructions are like a recipe read aloud — skip or mishear one step, and the whole result can go wrong, even if you understood every other step perfectly.

Tips for following instructions

TipWhy it helps
Listen for ordering words“First,” “then,” “after that,” “finally” signal the sequence
Note any conditions“If you are under 18, sign here instead” changes what to do
Expect a specific actionInstructions usually ask you to write, tick, circle, or select something
Don't panic on one missed wordKeep listening; context often fills the gap

Why this matters to you

Form- and instruction-based questions are common throughout IELTS Listening, especially in Section 1 — correctly understanding the sequence and any conditions directly determines whether your answer is marked correct.

🧪 Try it yourself: Ask someone to give you three step-by-step spoken instructions for a simple task (like making tea), and try following them exactly as described.

🔑 Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Sequence

The specific order steps must be followed in

Condition

A rule that changes what to do in a specific situation

Study tip: Listen for ordering words like “first” and “then” — they're your clearest signal for exactly where you are in a sequence of instructions.

lessons.title: 5.1 Note Completion Practice
lessons.html:
Note Completion PracticeLesson note
🤔 Let's start with a question
You're given a partly-written summary with blank spaces, and must fill each one in using only what you hear. Sounds simple — so why do people lose marks here?

Note Completion Practice

In plain words

Note completion means filling in missing words or numbers in a partial summary, using exactly the words you hear in a recording, no more and no fewer.

Note completion is like filling in the blanks of a partly-erased letter — the surrounding words are already there to guide you, but you must supply exactly the missing piece, not a rephrased version of it.

Tips for note completion

TipWhy it matters
Check the word limit“No more than two words” means exactly that — not three
Use the surrounding words as cluesThey tell you what type of word (noun, number, name) fits
Write exactly what you hearDon't change the speaker's actual words unless asked to
Check spellingAn answer with a spelling mistake is usually marked wrong

Why this matters to you

Note completion is one of the most common IELTS Listening question types across every section — strictly following the word limit and writing exactly what is said are the two most common reasons students lose otherwise-earned marks.

🧪 Try it yourself: Write three sentences with one word missing from each, then have someone read a matching word aloud for you to fill in the blank correctly.

🔑 Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Word limit

The maximum number of words allowed in an answer, stated in the question

Verbatim

Written exactly as spoken, without changing the wording

Study tip: Always check the word limit before you start listening — writing three words when only two are allowed will cost you the mark, even if the words themselves are correct.

lessons.title: 6.1 Form Completion Practice
lessons.html:
Form Completion PracticeLesson note
🤔 Let's start with a question
A recording gives someone's booking details — name, phone number, date, and request — and you must fill out a form exactly as they say it. What's the trickiest part?

Form Completion Practice

In plain words

Form completion means listening to a conversation, often a booking or registration, and filling in a form with the correct personal details.

Filling out a form from listening is like being the receptionist taking down a real booking over the phone — every detail (name, date, request) must be captured accurately, because someone will rely on this form later.

Tips for form completion

TipWhy it matters
Look at the form's headings firstThey tell you exactly what information to expect (name, date, phone)
Expect spelling and numbersNames and phone numbers are almost always spelled/said aloud
Watch for correctionsSpeakers often correct a detail partway through
Match the exact format asked forA date might need to be written as “12 August” not “August 12”

Why this matters to you

Form completion is a classic IELTS Listening Section 1 task, directly combining the earlier skills of names, numbers, and instructions into one realistic, practical task — exactly the kind of situation you might face in real life too.

🧪 Try it yourself: Draw a simple form with blanks for Name, Date, and Phone Number, then have someone give you those details aloud (with one correction) for you to fill in.

🔑 Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Form heading

The label on a form telling you what information belongs there

Registration

The process of officially recording someone's details

Study tip: Reading the form's headings before the recording starts tells you exactly what type of information is coming, which makes it far easier to catch it in time.

lessons.title: 1.1 Skimming and Scanning
lessons.html:
Skimming and ScanningLesson note
🤔 Let's start with a question
You have twenty minutes to answer questions about a two-page article. Do you really have time to read every single word carefully?

Skimming and Scanning

In plain words

Skimming means reading quickly to get the general idea of a text. Scanning means searching quickly for one specific piece of information, like a name or date.

Skimming is like flying over a city to see its general layout; scanning is like zooming in on your phone's map to find one exact street address — two different speeds for two different jobs.

Skimming vs. scanning

SkimmingScanning
GoalUnderstand the general ideaFind one specific detail
SpeedFast, reading the whole text looselyVery fast, ignoring everything except the target
When to useBefore answering questions, to get an overviewWhen looking for a specific name, number, or word

Why this matters to you

IELTS Reading gives you far too little time to read every word carefully — skimming for the overall idea first, then scanning for specific answers, is the core time-management strategy nearly every high scorer relies on.

🧪 Try it yourself: Take any short article and practice: skim it in 30 seconds to summarise its main idea, then scan it in 10 seconds to find one specific date or name.

🔑 Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Skimming

Reading quickly for a general understanding

Scanning

Searching quickly for one specific piece of information

Study tip: Always skim a passage first for the general idea before you even look at the questions — it makes scanning for specific answers afterward far faster and more accurate.

lessons.title: 2.1 Finding Main Ideas
lessons.html:
Finding Main IdeasLesson note
🤔 Let's start with a question
A paragraph has ten sentences, but only one core idea. Could you point to that one idea if asked right now?

Finding Main Ideas

In plain words

Finding the main idea means identifying the single most important point a paragraph or passage is making, separate from all its supporting details.

A paragraph is like a courtroom argument: one main claim, supported by evidence. Finding the main idea means spotting the actual claim, not getting distracted by all the supporting evidence around it.

Where main ideas usually hide

LocationWhy it's likely there
The first sentence of a paragraphOften introduces the topic directly
The last sentence of a paragraphSometimes summarises or concludes the point
Repeated words or ideasIdeas mentioned several times are usually central

Why this matters to you

IELTS Reading regularly tests main idea recognition directly, through “matching headings” or general comprehension questions — being able to state a paragraph's core point in one sentence is a foundational reading skill for the whole exam.

🧪 Try it yourself: Read any paragraph from a book or article and try to summarise its main idea in a single sentence of your own.

🔑 Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Main idea

The single most important point a text is making

Supporting detail

Extra information that explains or backs up the main idea

Study tip: If you're unsure of a paragraph's main idea, check its very first and very last sentences first — the answer is often hiding in one of those two places.

lessons.title: 3.1 Reading Advertisements
lessons.html:
Reading AdvertisementsLesson note
🤔 Let's start with a question
An advert for a job or a product is full of persuasive, exciting language. But underneath that, what are the actual, factual details?

Reading Advertisements

In plain words

Reading advertisements means understanding both the persuasive language used to attract attention, and the actual factual details — price, requirements, contact information — hidden inside.

An advertisement is like a colourful shop window display: exciting to look at, but the real facts you need (the price tag, the size, the material) are usually written in smaller text nearby.

What to look for in an ad

ElementExample
Persuasive language“Amazing offer!”, “Don't miss out!”
Factual detailsPrice, dates, requirements, contact details
Conditions“Only while stocks last”, “Applicants must be 18+”

Why this matters to you

IELTS Reading (especially General Training) includes real-world texts like advertisements and notices — questions usually test whether you can extract the actual factual details, not just notice the exciting language surrounding them.

🧪 Try it yourself: Find a real advertisement (online or in a newspaper) and list three factual details hidden inside its persuasive language.

🔑 Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Persuasive language

Words designed to convince or excite a reader

Condition

A rule or requirement attached to an offer

Study tip: When reading an advertisement, mentally separate the exciting language from the plain facts — the questions almost always test the facts, not the excitement.

lessons.title: 4.1 Reading Emails and Messages
lessons.html:
Reading Emails and MessagesLesson note
🤔 Let's start with a question
An email arrives with several paragraphs, but really only one or two sentences contain the action you actually need to take. Can you spot them quickly?

Reading Emails and Messages

In plain words

Reading emails and messages means understanding the sender's purpose and any action required, even within casual or informal writing.

An email is like a short conversation on paper: somewhere inside the polite opening and closing, there's usually one real request or piece of information — your job is to find it quickly.

What to look for in an email

ElementPurpose
Greeting/closingSets the tone (formal or informal)
The main request or updateThe actual reason the email was sent
Any deadline or dateWhen something needs to happen
ToneCan reveal urgency, friendliness, or formality

Why this matters to you

IELTS General Training Reading includes everyday texts like emails and messages — questions often ask you to identify the sender's main purpose or a specific detail like a date, so quickly finding the real point of the message is essential.

🧪 Try it yourself: Look back at a real email or message you've received recently and identify its one main purpose in a single sentence.

🔑 Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Purpose

The main reason a message was written

Tone

The overall feeling or formality of a piece of writing

Study tip: Read the first and last lines of an email first — the true purpose is very often stated clearly in one of those two places.

lessons.title: 5.1 Reading Short Articles
lessons.html:
Reading Short ArticlesLesson note
🤔 Let's start with a question
A short news article covers a real event in just a few paragraphs. Could you explain what happened, and why it matters, after just one read?

Reading Short Articles

In plain words

Reading short articles means understanding the key facts of a news or informational piece: what happened, who was involved, and why it matters.

A short article is like a news reporter's summary at the start of a broadcast — it packs the most important facts (who, what, when, why) into a small space, and your job is to extract them efficiently.

Key questions to answer while reading

QuestionWhat it reveals
Who?The people or organisations involved
What?The event or topic itself
When/where?The time and place
Why does it matter?The significance or consequence

Why this matters to you

IELTS Reading passages are often structured like short articles, especially in the earlier, easier sections — practising these “who, what, when, why” questions builds the exact comprehension skill the test rewards.

🧪 Try it yourself: Read a short news article and answer the four key questions (who, what, when/where, why it matters) in your own words.

🔑 Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Significance

Why an event or fact actually matters

Key fact

An essential piece of information a text is built around

Study tip: Practising the “who, what, when, why” questions on any short text you read builds a comprehension habit that transfers directly to IELTS Reading passages.

lessons.title: 6.1 Vocabulary Building
lessons.html:
Vocabulary BuildingLesson note
🤔 Let's start with a question
You understand a reading passage's grammar perfectly, but three key words are completely unfamiliar. Does the whole passage still make sense?

Vocabulary Building

In plain words

Vocabulary building for reading means actively growing the range of words you recognise, especially words common in real articles, notices, and academic texts.

Building reading vocabulary is like slowly filling a toolbox — every new word you learn is one more tool ready for the next passage, so unfamiliar texts become less intimidating over time.

Effective vocabulary-building habits

HabitWhy it helps
Keep a personal word listWrite down new words you meet while reading, with their meaning
Guess from context firstTry to work out a word's meaning from the sentence before checking a dictionary
Learn words in topic groupsWords about the same subject reinforce each other in memory
Review regularlyRevisiting old words keeps them from being forgotten

Why this matters to you

A wider reading vocabulary directly reduces how often you get stuck on unfamiliar words during the actual IELTS Reading test, and it also strengthens your Writing and Speaking vocabulary at the same time.

🧪 Try it yourself: While reading anything today, write down two unfamiliar words, guess their meaning from context, then check if you were right.

🔑 Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Context

The surrounding words and sentences that help explain an unfamiliar word

Word list

A personal, growing collection of new vocabulary and meanings

Study tip: Before reaching for a dictionary, always try guessing a word's meaning from its surrounding sentence first — this is exactly the skill IELTS Reading rewards, since you won't have a dictionary in the real exam.
