lessons.title: 1.1 Sentence Writing
lessons.html:
Sentence WritingLesson note
🤔 Let's start with a question
You know plenty of English words. But putting them on paper as a correct, complete sentence — is that a different skill entirely?

Sentence Writing

In plain words

Sentence writing means putting words together on paper into a grammatically correct, complete sentence that clearly expresses one idea.

Writing a sentence is like building one solid brick before building a wall — every longer piece of writing you'll ever do in IELTS is built from correctly written sentences just like this one.

What every written sentence needs

RequirementExample
A subject and a verb“The market opens early.”
Correct punctuationStarts with a capital letter, ends with a full stop
One complete ideaNot a fragment like “Because it was raining.”

Why this matters to you

Every piece of IELTS Writing, from Task 1 to Task 2, is built entirely from individual sentences — if your basic sentences aren't grammatically solid, no amount of good ideas can raise your score, since accuracy is marked directly.

🧪 Try it yourself: Write three complete sentences about your day, checking each one has a subject, a verb, correct punctuation, and expresses one full idea.

🔑 Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Sentence

A group of words expressing one complete idea, with a subject and verb

Fragment

An incomplete piece of writing that is not a full sentence

Study tip: Read your own sentences back out loud — if a sentence sounds incomplete or confusing when spoken, it usually needs fixing before you move on.

lessons.title: 2.1 Paragraph Writing
lessons.html:
Paragraph WritingLesson note
🤔 Let's start with a question
You've written five separate, correct sentences. Do they automatically form one clear paragraph, or does something else need to connect them?

Paragraph Writing

In plain words

Paragraph writing means grouping related sentences together around one main idea, so they read as one connected, organised block of writing.

A paragraph is like a small team working toward one shared goal: every sentence should support the same main idea, the way every player on a team supports the same game plan.

Building a strong paragraph

PartPurpose
Topic sentenceStates the paragraph's main idea, usually first
Supporting sentencesExplain or give examples for the main idea
Linking wordsConnect ideas smoothly, like “for example” or “however”

Why this matters to you

IELTS Writing Task 2 essays are built entirely from well-organised paragraphs, each with its own clear main idea — an essay with no clear paragraph structure loses marks for coherence, even if the individual sentences are grammatically fine.

🧪 Try it yourself: Write a short paragraph (3-4 sentences) about your hometown, starting with a clear topic sentence followed by supporting details.

🔑 Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Topic sentence

The sentence stating a paragraph's main idea, usually placed first

Linking word

A word connecting ideas smoothly, like “however” or “therefore”

Study tip: Start every paragraph with a clear topic sentence — it gives both you and the reader an instant anchor for what the rest of the paragraph will be about.

lessons.title: 3.1 Describing People
lessons.html:
Describing PeopleLesson note
🤔 Let's start with a question
You need to describe a person clearly in writing, not just speaking. Does describing someone on paper actually work differently from saying it out loud?

Describing People

In plain words

Describing people in writing means using clear, specific written vocabulary to describe someone's appearance and personality, organised into complete sentences and paragraphs.

Written description is like painting a portrait with words instead of a brush — the reader can't see the person, so your specific word choices are the only way they can picture them accurately.

Structuring a written description

Paragraph focusExample content
IntroductionWho the person is and your relationship to them
AppearanceHeight, hair, general look
PersonalityCharacter traits, with a small example

Why this matters to you

IELTS Writing sometimes includes describing a person as part of a letter or narrative task, and this same descriptive vocabulary and structure is directly reusable in Speaking Part 2 as well.

🧪 Try it yourself: Write a short, three-paragraph description of someone you know, following the structure in the table above.

🔑 Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Descriptive vocabulary

Specific words used to paint a clear picture of someone or something

Structure

The organised order ideas are presented in

Study tip: Because a reader can't hear your tone of voice, choose your written words even more carefully than you would in speech — precision matters more on paper.

lessons.title: 4.1 Describing Places
lessons.html:
Describing PlacesLesson note
🤔 Let's start with a question
You want to describe your hometown in writing so vividly that someone who has never visited could picture it clearly. Where do you even start?

Describing Places

In plain words

Describing places in writing means using specific vocabulary about location, atmosphere, and features to help a reader clearly picture a place they've never seen.

Describing a place well is like being a tour guide through words alone — you highlight the sights, sounds, and feeling of a place so vividly that the reader feels like they've actually walked through it.

What a strong place description includes

ElementExample
Location“a small town on the coast”
Physical featuresbuildings, streets, nature, weather
Atmospherebusy, peaceful, lively, quiet
Personal connectionwhy the place matters to you

Why this matters to you

IELTS Writing and Speaking both frequently ask you to describe a place — a city, a room, a country you'd like to visit — so building this specific descriptive vocabulary pays off across multiple parts of the test.

🧪 Try it yourself: Write a short paragraph describing your own neighbourhood, including at least one detail from each row of the table above.

🔑 Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Atmosphere

The overall feeling or mood of a place

Physical feature

A concrete, visible detail of a place, like a building or river

Study tip: Include at least one sensory detail — a sound, smell, or sight — in any place description; it makes the writing feel far more real and specific.

lessons.title: 5.1 Writing Informal Emails
lessons.html:
Writing Informal EmailsLesson note
🤔 Let's start with a question
You're writing to a friend, not a stranger in a suit. Should that email sound exactly the same as a formal business letter?

Writing Informal Emails

In plain words

Writing informal emails means writing to friends or family in a relaxed, friendly tone, while still being clear and well-organised.

An informal email is like a written version of a friendly chat — warmer and more relaxed than a formal letter, but it should still have a clear beginning, message, and ending so the reader isn't confused.

Structuring an informal email

PartExample
Greeting“Hi Grace,” or “Dear Grace,”
Opening line“How are you? I hope you're doing well.”
Main messageThe actual news, question, or request
Sign-off“Take care,” or “Best,” followed by your name

Why this matters to you

IELTS General Training Writing Task 1 often specifically asks for an informal letter to a friend or family member — using the right relaxed tone, rather than an overly formal one, is part of what the examiner is actually scoring.

🧪 Try it yourself: Write a short informal email to a friend, telling them about something interesting that happened to you recently.

🔑 Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Informal tone

A relaxed, friendly way of writing, suited to people you know well

Sign-off

The closing phrase and name at the end of a message

Study tip: Read your informal email back and ask: would I actually say this to a friend? If it sounds too stiff or formal, relax the wording.

lessons.title: 6.1 Common Grammar Errors
lessons.html:
Common Grammar ErrorsLesson note
🤔 Let's start with a question
You've written a whole paragraph, and it feels right. But are there small, repeated mistakes you make without even noticing?

Common Grammar Errors

In plain words

This topic covers the specific grammar errors that appear most often in learners' writing, so you can recognise and correct them in your own work.

Common errors are like a few loose stones on an otherwise solid path — small, but if you don't know where they are, you'll trip on the exact same ones every single time you write.

Frequent errors to watch for

ErrorCorrect version
“She go to school”“She goes to school” (subject-verb agreement)
“I have 20 years”“I am 20 years old”
“I am agree”“I agree”
“Advices”“Advice” (uncountable, no plural “s”)

Why this matters to you

Because certain errors repeat across so many learners' writing, examiners recognise them instantly — correcting just these few common patterns can measurably raise your IELTS Writing accuracy score without needing to learn anything new.

🧪 Try it yourself: Look back at something you've written recently (in this course or elsewhere) and check it against the four common errors in the table above.

🔑 Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Subject-verb agreement

Matching a verb correctly to its subject, like “she goes” not “she go”

Uncountable noun

A noun with no plural form, like “advice” or “information”

Study tip: Keep a short personal list of your own repeated mistakes — everyone tends to make the same few errors, and a personal list is the fastest way to stop making them.

lessons.title: 1.1 Self-Introduction
lessons.html:
Self-IntroductionLesson note
🤔 Let's start with a question
An examiner's very first question will almost certainly be “Can you tell me a little about yourself?” Do you already have a confident, natural answer ready?

Self-Introduction

In plain words

A self-introduction is a short, confident spoken summary of who you are — your name, background, and a little about your life — used to open a conversation.

A self-introduction is like the opening handshake of a conversation — brief, but it sets the tone for everything that follows, so a confident start matters more than it might seem.

Building a simple self-introduction

PartExample
Name“My name is Samuel.”
Background“I'm from Monrovia, Liberia.”
Current life“I'm currently studying computer literacy.”
A personal detail“In my free time, I enjoy playing football.”

Why this matters to you

The IELTS Speaking test always opens with questions about yourself — having a natural, well-practised self-introduction removes the nervousness of the first few seconds and lets you start the whole test with confidence.

🧪 Try it yourself: Say a 30-second self-introduction out loud right now, covering your name, background, current life, and one personal detail.

🔑 Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Self-introduction

A short spoken summary of who you are

Background

Information about where you're from or your general life story

Study tip: Practise your self-introduction until it feels completely natural and unrehearsed — a confident, relaxed start shapes the examiner's first impression of your whole performance.

lessons.title: 2.1 Talking About Family
lessons.html:
Talking About FamilyLesson note
🤔 Let's start with a question
“Tell me about your family” sounds simple. But could you actually speak about it fluently for a full thirty seconds without stopping?

Talking About Family

In plain words

Talking about family means describing the people in your household or close relatives, and your relationship with them, in clear spoken English.

Talking about family is like reading from a book you already know by heart — since this is genuinely your own life, the goal is simply expressing what you already know, clearly and fluently.

Useful family-talk structure

PartExample
Who is in your family“I live with my parents and two sisters.”
A detail about one person“My older sister works as a nurse.”
Your relationship“We are very close, and we talk every day.”

Why this matters to you

Family is one of the most common IELTS Speaking Part 1 topics — preparing genuine, specific details in advance means you'll never be caught with nothing natural to say when this exact, very likely topic comes up.

🧪 Try it yourself: Speak out loud about your family for thirty seconds, including who is in it, one specific detail, and your relationship with them.

🔑 Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Household

The people who live together in one home

Relationship

How you connect with or feel about another person

Study tip: Prepare two or three genuine, specific details about your real family in advance — specific truth is always easier to speak fluently about than a vague, generic answer.

lessons.title: 3.1 Talking About Hobbies
lessons.html:
Talking About HobbiesLesson note
🤔 Let's start with a question
“What do you like to do in your free time?” — is “I like reading” really enough of an answer, or does the examiner expect more?

Talking About Hobbies

In plain words

Talking about hobbies means describing an activity you enjoy, explaining what you do, and why you enjoy it, in more than just one short phrase.

A one-word hobby answer is like a menu with just a dish's name and no description — technically an answer, but it gives the examiner nothing to actually listen to or assess.

Expanding a hobby answer

PartExample
The hobby“I really enjoy playing football.”
How often/with whom“I play with my friends most weekends.”
Why you enjoy it“It helps me relax and stay fit.”

Why this matters to you

IELTS Speaking specifically rewards expanded, detailed answers over short ones — a one-word hobby answer gives the examiner nothing to score fluency or vocabulary on, while an expanded answer showcases exactly those skills.

🧪 Try it yourself: Speak for thirty seconds about a hobby you enjoy, covering what it is, how often you do it, and why you enjoy it.

🔑 Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Expand

To add extra detail and explanation to a short answer

Hobby

An activity done regularly for enjoyment

Study tip: Whenever you answer a Speaking question, add at least one “because” — explaining why is what turns a short answer into a fluent, well-developed one.

lessons.title: 4.1 Talking About School
lessons.html:
Talking About SchoolLesson note
🤔 Let's start with a question
“Tell me about your school or studies” is a nearly guaranteed IELTS Speaking question. Could you answer it confidently right now, in detail?

Talking About School

In plain words

Talking about school means describing your studies, subjects, or learning experience clearly, whether currently studying or reflecting on the past.

Talking about school is like giving a short, friendly tour of a place you know extremely well — the goal isn't impressive vocabulary, but simply clear, confident, genuine description.

Useful school-talk structure

PartExample
What you study“I'm currently studying computer literacy.”
What you enjoy“I especially enjoy the practical, hands-on lessons.”
A challenge“Sometimes managing my time is difficult.”

Why this matters to you

School and education are extremely common IELTS Speaking Part 1 topics — having genuine, ready details about your own studies means you can answer naturally and confidently the moment this near-certain topic arises.

🧪 Try it yourself: Speak for thirty seconds about your current or most recent studies, covering what you study, what you enjoy, and one challenge.

🔑 Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Studies

The subjects or course a person is currently learning

Challenge

A difficulty faced while doing something

Study tip: Including one honest challenge, alongside what you enjoy, actually makes an answer sound more natural and thoughtful than an answer that's all positive.

lessons.title: 5.1 Talking About Work
lessons.html:
Talking About WorkLesson note
🤔 Let's start with a question
“What kind of work do you do, or would like to do?” — even if you're not employed yet, is there still a strong way to answer this?

Talking About Work

In plain words

Talking about work means describing your job, your desired career, or your work experience clearly, whether you are currently employed, studying, or job-seeking.

Talking about work is like describing a role in a play you're either already performing or preparing for — the goal is explaining your part clearly, whether it's your current job or your intended future one.

Structuring a work-related answer

SituationExample answer approach
Currently employed“I work as a... My main responsibilities are...”
A student“I'm currently studying, but I hope to work in...”
Job-seeking“I'm currently looking for work in the field of...”

Why this matters to you

IELTS Speaking Part 1 commonly asks about work or study — being ready with a clear, honest answer for whichever situation genuinely applies to you avoids any awkward hesitation on this very likely topic.

🧪 Try it yourself: Speak for thirty seconds about your current work, studies, or desired career, using the structure that matches your real situation.

🔑 Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Responsibility

A duty or task that is part of a job

Career

A person's long-term path of work or profession

Study tip: Whatever your real situation, answer honestly and specifically — a genuine, specific answer about studying or job-seeking works just as well as one about current employment.

lessons.title: 6.1 Basic Fluency Practice
lessons.html:
Basic Fluency PracticeLesson note
🤔 Let's start with a question
You know the right words and grammar, but you still pause and hesitate a lot when speaking. Is that a knowledge problem, or something else entirely?

Basic Fluency Practice

In plain words

Fluency means speaking smoothly and at a natural pace, without long pauses or constant hesitation, even if occasional small mistakes happen.

Fluency is like walking versus stopping every few steps to check your feet — you can technically know how to walk perfectly, but constant hesitation still makes the whole walk look unsure and slow.

Building fluency

Practice methodWhy it helps
Speak for one minute without stoppingTrains you to keep going instead of freezing on a mistake
Record and listen to yourselfReveals your own pauses and hesitation patterns
Use simple filler phrases“Let me think for a moment” buys time naturally, without silence
Practise regularly, even aloneBuilds comfort with your own speaking voice

Why this matters to you

Fluency is scored directly and separately in IELTS Speaking — a fluent answer with one or two small grammar mistakes often scores better than a hesitant, broken answer that is technically more “correct” but far harder to follow.

🧪 Try it yourself: Choose any simple topic (like your weekend) and speak about it out loud for one full minute without stopping, even if you make small mistakes.

🔑 Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Fluency

Speaking smoothly and at a natural pace, without long hesitation

Filler phrase

A short phrase used to naturally buy thinking time, like “let me think”

Study tip: If you don't know the perfect word mid-sentence, keep going with a simpler one rather than stopping completely — momentum matters more than perfection for fluency.

lessons.title: 1.1 Multiple Choice Questions
lessons.html:
Multiple Choice QuestionsLesson note
🤔 Let's start with a question
You hear a recording once, then must pick the ONE correct answer from three tricky, similar-sounding options. What's the trap here?

Multiple Choice Questions

In plain words

Multiple choice questions in IELTS Listening give you three or four options and ask you to choose the one that correctly matches what you heard.

These questions are like a magician's trick — the wrong options are often deliberately similar to something actually said, designed to catch you if you only half-listen.

Strategy for multiple choice

StepWhy it helps
Read all options before listeningYou know exactly what to listen for
Listen for the exact meaning, not just matching wordsA wrong option often reuses words from the recording out of context
Eliminate options you're sure are wrongNarrows your choice even if you're unsure of the right one
Choose based on the whole sentence, not one wordDistractors often twist just one detail

Why this matters to you

Multiple choice appears throughout every section of IELTS Listening — recognising that wrong options often reuse real words from the recording (just in the wrong context) is the single most useful strategy for avoiding this common trap.

🧪 Try it yourself: Listen to any short recording, pause it, and write down one word you heard that could easily be used to create a tempting but wrong multiple-choice option.

🔑 Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Distractor

A wrong answer option deliberately designed to seem correct

Eliminate

To rule out an option you're confident is incorrect

Study tip: Never choose an answer just because you heard one matching word — always check that the FULL meaning of the option matches what was actually said.

lessons.title: 2.1 Map Labelling
lessons.html:
Map LabellingLesson note
🤔 Let's start with a question
A recording describes a route across a map while you follow along and mark specific locations. How do you avoid getting completely lost partway through?

Map Labelling

In plain words

Map labelling means listening to spoken directions and correctly marking locations, routes, or features onto a given map or floor plan.

Map labelling is like being guided through a maze by someone else's voice alone — you must carefully track every turn as it's described, since missing one instruction can throw off everything after it.

Strategy for map labelling

StepWhy it helps
Study the map before listeningNotice key landmarks and possible starting points
Follow a finger or pen along the map as you listenKeeps your physical position matched to the description
Listen for direction words“Left,” “right,” “opposite,” “next to” are the key signals
Don't panic if you lose your place brieflyLandmarks mentioned later can help you catch up

Why this matters to you

Map labelling is a distinctive IELTS Listening question type that tests real-time spatial understanding — practising with real maps builds the specific skill of turning spoken directions into an accurate mental (or drawn) picture.

🧪 Try it yourself: Look at any simple map (even a hand-drawn one) and have someone describe a route across it while you trace it with your finger.

🔑 Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Floor plan

A map-like diagram showing the layout of a building

Direction word

A word like “left,” “right,” or “opposite” showing position or movement

Study tip: Studying the map for a few seconds before listening — noticing key landmarks and the likely starting point — makes it far easier to follow the spoken route without getting lost.

lessons.title: 3.1 Table Completion
lessons.html:
Table CompletionLesson note
🤔 Let's start with a question
A table has three columns and several empty cells. The recording gives all the missing details, but only once. What's the trickiest part of filling this in accurately?

Table Completion

In plain words

Table completion means listening to a recording and filling in missing information into the correct cells of a table, matching the exact category of each column.

A table is like a set of labelled boxes waiting to be filled — each answer must go into exactly the right box, in exactly the right form, or it doesn't count, however correct the actual word might be.

Strategy for table completion

StepWhy it helps
Study the column headings firstTells you exactly what type of information each column expects
Predict the type of word neededA “Price” column expects a number, a “Name” column expects a name
Follow the table's row orderThe recording usually follows the same order as the table
Check the word limitJust like note completion, strict limits apply

Why this matters to you

Table completion is common across every part of IELTS Listening and combines several earlier skills — reading headings, predicting word types, and following a sequence — into one realistic, structured task.

🧪 Try it yourself: Draw a simple three-column table (Name, Date, Reason) and have someone give you matching details aloud for you to fill in correctly.

🔑 Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Column heading

The label at the top of a table column, showing what type of data belongs there

Predict

To guess in advance what type of answer is likely needed

Study tip: Column headings are your biggest clue — a column called “Price” tells you a number is coming before you've even heard it.

lessons.title: 4.1 Sentence Completion
lessons.html:
Sentence CompletionLesson note
🤔 Let's start with a question
A sentence has one gap, and only the exact word or short phrase from the recording will fit correctly. How much freedom do you actually have here?

Sentence Completion

In plain words

Sentence completion means filling in a single missing word or short phrase within a given sentence, using the exact wording from the recording.

A sentence completion gap is like the missing puzzle piece in a picture — there's only one piece that truly fits, and forcing in a similar-but-wrong one leaves the picture visibly incomplete.

Strategy for sentence completion

StepWhy it helps
Read the sentence before listeningUnderstand exactly what kind of word is missing
Check the grammar around the gapA gap after “a” usually needs a singular noun
Write only what's neededStick strictly to the stated word limit
Check spelling carefullyAn otherwise correct answer can be marked wrong if misspelled

Why this matters to you

Sentence completion appears in Listening Section 2 tasks (like tour or event information) — using grammar clues around the gap to predict the missing word type is one of the most reliable ways to avoid guessing blindly.

🧪 Try it yourself: Write a sentence with one word missing (like “The museum opens at ___ o'clock”) and have someone say a matching detail for you to correctly insert.

🔑 Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Gap

The blank space in a sentence where a missing word or phrase belongs

Grammar clue

A hint from the sentence's structure about what type of word fits

Study tip: Look at the words immediately before and after the gap — they often reveal whether a noun, number, or short phrase is expected, even before you hear the answer.

lessons.title: 5.1 Summary Completion
lessons.html:
Summary CompletionLesson note
🤔 Let's start with a question
A whole paragraph summarises a longer recording, but with several words missing throughout. Can you catch every gap correctly across a longer stretch of listening?

Summary Completion

In plain words

Summary completion means filling in several missing words across a longer written summary of a recording, testing sustained listening over a bigger stretch of audio.

A summary completion task is like following a long story with several missing chapters — you must stay focused across the whole telling, not just for one short moment, to catch every missing piece.

Strategy for summary completion

StepWhy it helps
Read the whole summary firstUnderstand its overall topic and structure before listening
Underline key words near each gapThese are your listening targets as the recording plays
Stay in the correct orderThe summary usually follows the same order as the recording
Don't get stuck on one missed gapMove on and catch the next one; you can return later if time allows

Why this matters to you

Summary completion demands sustained concentration across a longer piece of audio, often in Listening Section 3 or 4 — reading the full summary first gives your brain a “map” of what's coming, which makes staying on track far easier.

🧪 Try it yourself: Read a short paragraph with three words removed, then have someone read a related passage aloud so you can fill in the three gaps correctly.

🔑 Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Summary

A shortened version of a longer text or recording, covering its main points

Sustained concentration

The ability to stay focused across a long stretch of listening or reading

Study tip: If you miss one gap, don't freeze — mentally note it and keep following the recording, since the next gap is often still catchable if you stay focused.

lessons.title: 6.1 Academic Listening
lessons.html:
Academic ListeningLesson note
🤔 Let's start with a question
A university lecture recording is longer, more formal, and uses more complex vocabulary than a casual conversation. Does your listening strategy need to change for this?

Academic Listening

In plain words

Academic listening means understanding longer, more formal spoken material, like lectures or presentations, which use more complex vocabulary and structure than everyday conversation.

Academic listening is like watching a documentary instead of a casual chat show — the pace is steadier and the content denser, so following the overall structure matters more than catching every single word.

Strategies for academic listening

StrategyWhy it helps
Listen for the lecture's structure“Firstly,” “in contrast,” “to conclude” signal the organisation
Focus on the main argument, not every detailAcademic talks are dense; you can't catch everything
Note key terms as they're introducedOften defined once, then referred to again later
Expect a formal, structured styleDifferent rhythm from casual daily conversation

Why this matters to you

IELTS Listening Section 4 typically features a lecture-style academic monologue — this is usually considered the hardest section, so practising with academic-style audio (like documentaries or online lectures) builds real familiarity with its particular pace and structure.

🧪 Try it yourself: Watch or listen to a short educational video and try to identify its introduction, two main points, and conclusion.

🔑 Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Lecture

A formal, structured spoken presentation on an academic topic

Structure word

A word like “firstly” or “in conclusion” signalling the organisation of a talk

Study tip: Listen for structure words like “firstly” and “to conclude” — they act as signposts, telling you exactly where you are within the overall lecture.

lessons.title: 1.1 Matching Headings
lessons.html:
Matching HeadingsLesson note
🤔 Let's start with a question
A passage has six paragraphs and a list of possible headings for each. Could you match every heading correctly without reading every single word?

Matching Headings

In plain words

Matching headings means choosing the heading that best summarises each paragraph's main idea, from a list of options provided.

This task is like matching chapter titles to chapters in a book you've only skimmed — you don't need every detail, just a strong sense of what each section is mainly about.

Strategy for matching headings

StepWhy it helps
Skim each paragraph for its main idea firstYou need the overall point, not every detail
Read all heading options before decidingSome headings are deliberately similar to trick you
Watch for headings that only match one small detailA good heading covers the WHOLE paragraph, not just one sentence
Match easier paragraphs firstLeaves fewer, harder options for the trickiest paragraphs

Why this matters to you

Matching headings is one of the more challenging IELTS Reading question types, since it directly tests main-idea recognition (from earlier in this course) across an entire passage rather than just one paragraph.

🧪 Try it yourself: Take any article with several paragraphs and write your own one-line heading for each, before checking whether they truly summarise the whole paragraph.

🔑 Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Heading

A short title summarising a paragraph's main idea

Overall idea

The main point of an entire paragraph, not just one detail within it

Study tip: Always ask “does this heading cover the WHOLE paragraph?” — a heading matching only one small detail is a very common trap in this question type.

lessons.title: 2.1 True/False/Not Given
lessons.html:
True/False/Not GivenLesson note
🤔 Let's start with a question
A statement seems to match the passage, but the passage never actually says whether it's true or false at all. What do you write?

True/False/Not Given

In plain words

True/False/Not Given asks whether a statement agrees with the passage (True), contradicts it (False), or simply isn't mentioned at all (Not Given).

This task is like being a fact-checker: True means the article confirms it, False means the article says the opposite, and Not Given means the article simply never brings up the topic at all, either way.

Telling the three apart

AnswerWhat it means
TrueThe passage clearly states or confirms this
FalseThe passage clearly states the opposite
Not GivenThe passage never actually mentions this specific point, either way

Why this matters to you

“Not Given” is the answer most learners get wrong, often because they assume something is False when the passage simply never mentions it at all — recognising the difference between “opposite” and “absent” is the real skill this question type tests.

🧪 Try it yourself: Take three statements about any short passage: write one clearly True, one clearly False, and one that is simply Not Given, based on that passage.

🔑 Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Contradict

To say the exact opposite of something

Not Given

When a passage simply never mentions a specific point at all

Study tip: Before choosing False, ask yourself: does the passage actually say the OPPOSITE, or does it just not mention this at all? Only a true opposite counts as False.

lessons.title: 3.1 Yes/No/Not Given
lessons.html:
Yes/No/Not GivenLesson note
🤔 Let's start with a question
This looks just like True/False/Not Given. So why does IELTS actually use two separate versions of what seems like the exact same question type?

Yes/No/Not Given

In plain words

Yes/No/Not Given works the same way as True/False/Not Given, but specifically tests whether a statement matches the writer's opinions or claims, rather than pure facts.

If True/False/Not Given is fact-checking a news report, Yes/No/Not Given is fact-checking someone's personal opinion column — the same three-way logic applies, just aimed at views and arguments instead of plain facts.

When each version is used

Question typeUsed for
True/False/Not GivenFactual, informational passages
Yes/No/Not GivenPassages with opinions, arguments, or claims

Why this matters to you

Recognising which version applies (usually stated in the instructions) tells you whether to focus on checking hard facts or the writer's personal stance — a small distinction that changes exactly what you should be scanning for.

🧪 Try it yourself: Find an opinion piece or persuasive article and write one statement that matches the writer's view (Yes), one that contradicts it (No), and one they never actually address (Not Given).

🔑 Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Writer's opinion

What the author personally believes or argues, as opposed to plain fact

Claim

A statement the writer is arguing is true

Study tip: Always check the instructions carefully — they tell you clearly whether you're being asked about facts (True/False) or the writer's opinions (Yes/No).

lessons.title: 4.1 Matching Information
lessons.html:
Matching InformationLesson note
🤔 Let's start with a question
A question asks “In which paragraph is X mentioned?” — the passage has eight paragraphs. Do you have to read all of them carefully to find it?

Matching Information

In plain words

Matching information means identifying which specific paragraph of a passage contains a particular piece of information or detail.

This task is like finding which chapter of a long book mentions a specific event — you don't need to reread the whole book, just scan efficiently for the specific detail requested.

Strategy for matching information

StepWhy it helps
Identify the key word(s) in the questionThese are exactly what you'll scan for
Scan quickly, don't read fullyYou're hunting for a specific detail, not understanding everything
Watch for synonymsThe passage may use a different word with the same meaning
Confirm the whole idea matches, not just one wordA matching word alone doesn't guarantee it's the right paragraph

Why this matters to you

Matching information tests targeted scanning under time pressure — since IELTS passages are often long, efficiently locating just the relevant paragraph (rather than reading everything closely) is a critical time-saving skill.

🧪 Try it yourself: Take a multi-paragraph article and, without reading it fully, scan quickly to find which paragraph mentions one specific detail (like a date or a name).

🔑 Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Synonym

A different word with a similar or the same meaning

Targeted scanning

Searching quickly for one specific piece of information

Study tip: Before scanning, think of two or three synonyms for your key word — the passage may express the same idea using completely different vocabulary.

lessons.title: 5.1 Sentence Completion
lessons.html:
Sentence CompletionLesson note
🤔 Let's start with a question
Just like in Listening, a Reading passage has a sentence with a gap. But now you must find the missing word yourself, directly from the passage. How is that different?

Sentence Completion

In plain words

In Reading, sentence completion means filling a gap in a given sentence using words taken directly from the passage, matching both the meaning and the stated word limit.

This is like finding one missing puzzle piece hidden somewhere across an entire picture, rather than just being handed it — you must first locate the correct part of the passage before you can even see what fits.

Strategy for sentence completion in Reading

StepWhy it helps
Identify key words in the incomplete sentenceThese help you scan the passage for the matching section
Find the exact matching part of the passageThe answer's exact wording usually appears there
Copy the wording exactlyChanging the passage's own words can mark an answer wrong
Check the word limit and grammar fitThe answer must grammatically complete the sentence correctly

Why this matters to you

Unlike Listening, Reading sentence completion lets you look back at the exact passage text as many times as needed — the real skill here is efficiently locating the right section, not catching something on a single, unrepeatable listen.

🧪 Try it yourself: Take a paragraph and write one sentence with a word missing that could be answered by copying an exact word or phrase from that same paragraph.

🔑 Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Exact wording

Using the passage's own words precisely, without changing them

Key word

A specific, distinctive word used to help locate information

Study tip: Always copy the exact words from the passage rather than rephrasing them in your own words — sentence completion in Reading specifically rewards precise copying, not paraphrasing.

lessons.title: 6.1 Diagram Labelling
lessons.html:
Diagram LabellingLesson note
🤔 Let's start with a question
A passage describes a machine or a process, and a diagram beside it has empty labels. Can you match the written description to the correct part of the picture?

Diagram Labelling

In plain words

Diagram labelling means reading a passage describing an object or process, and correctly labelling the corresponding parts of a diagram using words from the text.

This task is like assembling furniture using written instructions and a picture together — the words explain what each part is, and the diagram shows you exactly where that part belongs.

Strategy for diagram labelling

StepWhy it helps
Study the diagram before reading closelyUnderstand its overall shape and any labels already given
Find the section of text describing each partUsually organised in the same order as the diagram
Match technical vocabulary carefullyDiagrams often involve precise, specific words
Check spelling of copied labelsJust like other completion tasks, exact spelling matters

Why this matters to you

Diagram labelling most often appears in Academic Reading passages describing scientific or technical processes — it tests whether you can connect written description directly to a visual, a skill useful well beyond the exam itself.

🧪 Try it yourself: Find a simple diagram (like a plant or a household object) with unlabelled parts, and write a short description that would help someone else label it correctly.

🔑 Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Diagram

A drawing or picture showing the parts or structure of something

Label

A word or short phrase identifying a specific part of a diagram

Study tip: Look at the diagram first and predict roughly what each unlabelled part might be — it gives you a head start before you even begin reading the detailed description.

lessons.title: 7.1 Reading Academic Texts
lessons.html:
Reading Academic TextsLesson note
🤔 Let's start with a question
An academic passage uses long, formal sentences and specialised vocabulary. Does it need a completely different reading approach than a newspaper article?

Reading Academic Texts

In plain words

Reading academic texts means understanding longer, more formal, and more complex passages — often on scientific or research topics — using all the reading strategies built earlier in this course.

Academic texts are like a more complex, denser meal than a snack — the same basic eating (reading) skills apply, but you naturally slow down, pace yourself, and pay more attention.

Approaching academic texts

StrategyWhy it helps
Skim first for the overall topic and structureAcademic passages are often organised into clear, labelled stages
Don't panic at unfamiliar technical wordsOften explained or clarified within the passage itself
Watch for the writer's argument or findingsAcademic passages often present a specific claim or result
Use all previous strategies togetherSkimming, scanning, and main-idea finding all still apply

Why this matters to you

IELTS Academic Reading is built almost entirely from passages like this — bringing together every strategy from this whole module (skimming, scanning, main ideas, vocabulary) is exactly what's needed to handle these denser, more formal texts confidently.

🧪 Try it yourself: Find a short academic-style article (a science news piece works well) and identify its main topic, one key finding, and one unfamiliar word you worked out from context.

🔑 Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Academic text

A formal piece of writing, often about research, science, or scholarly topics

Finding

A specific result or conclusion reported in an academic passage

Study tip: Academic texts reward patience more than speed — skim first for the shape of the whole argument, then read the specific sections the questions actually ask about.

lessons.title: 1.1 Introduction to Task 1
lessons.html:
Introduction to Task 1Lesson note
🤔 Let's start with a question
Task 1 gives you a chart, graph, or diagram and asks you to describe it — not give your opinion. Why is that distinction so important?

Introduction to Task 1

In plain words

Task 1 requires you to objectively describe visual information (charts, graphs, tables, or diagrams) in your own words, without giving any personal opinion.

Task 1 is like being a neutral news reporter describing what a graph shows, not a commentator arguing whether the trend is good or bad — your job is accurate description, not judgment.

The basic structure of a Task 1 response

PartPurpose
IntroductionParaphrase what the chart/graph shows
OverviewState the main overall trend(s) or key features
Body paragraphsDescribe specific data with supporting figures

Why this matters to you

Task 1 is worth exactly as much as Task 2 toward your Writing band score, yet many learners under-practise it — mastering its specific, objective structure is a quick and reliable way to raise your overall Writing score.

🧪 Try it yourself: Look at any simple chart or graph (even one from a newspaper) and write one sentence objectively describing its main overall trend, with no personal opinion included.

🔑 Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Objective description

Describing facts without adding personal opinion

Overview

A summary of the main trend(s) shown in a chart or graph

Study tip: Always include a clear overview stating the main trend — many learners jump straight into small details and forget this crucial big-picture sentence, which examiners specifically look for.

lessons.title: 2.1 Charts and Graphs
lessons.html:
Charts and GraphsLesson note
🤔 Let's start with a question
A bar chart, a line graph, and a pie chart all show numbers — but do you describe each one using exactly the same language?

Charts and Graphs

In plain words

This topic covers the general vocabulary and approach for describing charts and graphs, the most common visual types in Writing Task 1.

Different chart types are like different sports — they share the same general idea (competition, or in this case, showing data), but each has its own specific rules and language for describing what's happening.

General chart-describing vocabulary

VocabularyUse
Increase / rise / growNumbers going up
Decrease / fall / declineNumbers going down
Remain stable / stay constantNumbers staying the same
FluctuateNumbers going up and down repeatedly

Why this matters to you

This shared vocabulary applies across nearly every chart type you'll meet in Task 1 — learning it thoroughly here saves you from needing to relearn basic describing language separately for every specific chart type covered next.

🧪 Try it yourself: Look at any chart with rising and falling data and describe it out loud using at least three words from the table above.

🔑 Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Trend

The general direction data moves in over time

Fluctuate

To rise and fall repeatedly and irregularly

Study tip: Build a personal list of trend vocabulary (increase, decrease, fluctuate, plateau) — reusing the same reliable words confidently is better than reaching for unfamiliar ones under exam pressure.

lessons.title: 3.1 Tables
lessons.html:
TablesLesson note
🤔 Let's start with a question
A table Task 1 has no visual trend line at all — just rows and columns of numbers. How do you even begin describing something with no obvious “shape”?

Tables

In plain words

Describing tables in Task 1 means identifying which numbers are worth comparing and highlighting, since a table itself has no visual pattern to describe directly.

A table is like a spreadsheet with no chart drawn from it yet — your job is to mentally spot the patterns (highest, lowest, biggest difference) that a chart would normally show visually.

Approaching a table

StepWhy it helps
Find the highest and lowest figuresThese are usually worth highlighting first
Compare related rows or columnsLook for meaningful differences or similarities
Group similar figures togetherAvoid listing every single number one by one
Select the most significant dataYou cannot mention every number; choose the most notable ones

Why this matters to you

Table-based Task 1 questions require you to actively choose which numbers matter most, since there's no visual pattern doing that work for you — this selective-comparison skill is exactly what separates a strong table description from a robotic list of every figure.

🧪 Try it yourself: Find or create a simple table with 6-8 numbers and identify the highest, lowest, and one interesting comparison between two figures.

🔑 Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Significant

Notable or important enough to be worth mentioning

Comparison

Looking at the difference or similarity between two or more figures

Study tip: Never try to mention every number in a table — select the highest, lowest, and one or two meaningful comparisons instead, and group the rest where possible.

lessons.title: 4.1 Pie Charts
lessons.html:
Pie ChartsLesson note
🤔 Let's start with a question
A pie chart shows five slices of different sizes representing percentages. How do you describe “slices” in clear, natural written English?

Pie Charts

In plain words

Pie charts show data as proportional “slices” of a whole circle, usually representing percentages, and Task 1 requires describing the relative size of these slices.

A pie chart is like a whole pizza cut into differently-sized slices — your job is describing which slices are the biggest, smallest, and how they compare to each other, all in words.

Pie chart vocabulary

VocabularyExample
The largest/smallest proportion“The largest proportion was spent on housing.”
Account for“Housing accounted for 40% of spending.”
A quarter / a third / just under halfUseful rounded fraction language
Compared to / whereasFor comparing two different slices

Why this matters to you

Pie charts are one of the most common Task 1 visual types — the vocabulary above (proportions, fractions, comparisons) directly targets exactly the kind of description these slice-based charts require.

🧪 Try it yourself: Imagine a pie chart of your own weekly spending and describe, out loud, the largest and smallest “slices” using at least two phrases from the table above.

🔑 Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Proportion

A part or share of a whole amount

Account for

To make up a certain percentage or amount of a total

Study tip: Rounded fractions like “just under half” or “roughly a quarter” often sound more natural in written English than exact percentages repeated over and over.

lessons.title: 5.1 Line Graphs
lessons.html:
Line GraphsLesson note
🤔 Let's start with a question
A line graph shows a value changing across ten years. Should you describe every single year individually, or is there a smarter approach?

Line Graphs

In plain words

Line graphs show how a value changes over time, and Task 1 requires describing the overall trend and any notable individual changes.

A line graph is like a heartbeat monitor — what matters most is the overall pattern (steadily rising, spiking, falling) rather than obsessing over every single tiny beat along the way.

Line graph description approach

StepWhy it helps
Identify the overall trend firstRising, falling, or fluctuating over the whole period
Note the start and end pointsUseful for describing overall change
Highlight any sharp changeA sudden spike or drop is usually worth mentioning specifically
Use time-based language“Between 2010 and 2015,” “from 2018 onward”

Why this matters to you

Line graphs are extremely common in Task 1, especially showing things like population or sales over time — describing the overall trend first, then one or two specific notable points, is far more effective than a robotic year-by-year account.

🧪 Try it yourself: Imagine a line graph showing your own sleep hours over a week and describe its overall trend, plus one notable change, out loud.

🔑 Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Overall trend

The general pattern a line graph shows across the whole time period

Sharp change

A sudden, noticeable rise or fall in a graph

Study tip: Always state the overall trend in one clear sentence before diving into specific details — it gives the examiner an instant, correct impression of the whole graph.

lessons.title: 6.1 Bar Charts
lessons.html:
Bar ChartsLesson note
🤔 Let's start with a question
A bar chart compares five different countries' populations side by side. Is describing this really so different from a line graph showing change over time?

Bar Charts

In plain words

Bar charts use bars of different heights or lengths to compare separate categories, and Task 1 requires describing these comparisons clearly.

A bar chart is like a lineup of people of different heights standing side by side — your job is describing who is tallest, shortest, and how the others compare, rather than describing change over time.

Bar chart description approach

StepWhy it helps
Identify the highest and lowest barsThe most obvious, important comparisons
Group similar bars together“Three countries had roughly similar populations”
Use comparative language“Higher than,” “nearly double,” “significantly lower”
Avoid describing every bar individuallyFocus on the most meaningful comparisons only

Why this matters to you

Bar charts test comparison language specifically, differently from line graphs which test change-over-time language — recognising which type you're looking at tells you immediately which vocabulary set to reach for.

🧪 Try it yourself: Imagine a bar chart comparing five friends' heights and describe out loud who is tallest, shortest, and one meaningful comparison between two of them.

🔑 Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Comparative language

Words used to compare two or more things, like “higher than” or “nearly double”

Category

A separate group being compared, like a country or product type

Study tip: Bar charts reward strong comparative language — practise phrases like “nearly double,” “roughly half,” and “significantly higher than” until they feel natural.

lessons.title: 7.1 Process Diagrams
lessons.html:
Process DiagramsLesson note
🤔 Let's start with a question
A diagram shows the six steps of how a product is manufactured, with arrows connecting each stage. How do you turn a picture full of arrows into flowing written English?

Process Diagrams

In plain words

Process diagrams show a sequence of steps or stages, like manufacturing or a natural cycle, and Task 1 requires describing this sequence clearly and in order.

A process diagram is like a recipe shown as pictures with arrows instead of numbered steps — your job is turning that picture back into clear, ordered written instructions.

Describing a process

ElementExample language
Sequence words“First,” “next,” “after that,” “finally”
Passive voice“The material is heated,” rather than naming who does it
StagesClearly separate each step into its own sentence or short section
Beginning and endState where the process starts and where it finishes

Why this matters to you

Process diagrams are a distinctly different Task 1 type from charts and graphs — since there's no data or numbers involved, examiners specifically look for clear sequencing and correct use of the passive voice throughout your description.

🧪 Try it yourself: Think of a simple process you know well (like making tea) and describe its steps out loud using sequence words and passive voice where natural.

🔑 Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Sequence

The specific order steps happen in

Passive voice

A sentence structure focusing on the action, like “it is heated,” rather than who does it

Study tip: Practise passive voice sentences like “the water is boiled” or “the mixture is poured” — this structure is expected and rewarded in process diagram descriptions.

lessons.title: 8.1 Maps
lessons.html:
MapsLesson note
🤔 Let's start with a question
Two maps show the same town in 1990 and 2020, with new buildings and roads added. How do you describe change between two pictures, rather than a chart?

Maps

In plain words

Map tasks show one or two maps (often showing change over time) and require describing the layout, features, or changes between them.

Comparing two maps is like a “spot the difference” picture puzzle — your task is naming exactly what's new, what's gone, and what's stayed the same between the two versions.

Describing map changes

ElementExample language
New additions“A new school was built in the north of the town.”
Removed features“The old market was demolished.”
Unchanged features“The river remained in the same position.”
Location language“In the north,” “to the east of,” “near the centre”

Why this matters to you

Map tasks appear regularly in Task 1 and specifically test location vocabulary and change-describing language together — being comfortable with both compass directions and “before and after” phrasing covers exactly what this task type requires.

🧪 Try it yourself: Imagine your own neighbourhood ten years ago versus today, and describe out loud one change, using location language from the table above.

🔑 Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Demolish

To knock down or remove a building

Compass direction

North, south, east, or west, used to describe location

Study tip: Learn the compass directions (north, south, east, west) and simple location phrases (“to the east of,” “in the centre of”) thoroughly — they're used constantly in every map task.

lessons.title: 9.1 Comparing Data
lessons.html:
Comparing DataLesson note
🤔 Let's start with a question
Two lines on a graph almost cross each other, then separate again. How do you clearly explain a relationship like that in writing?

Comparing Data

In plain words

Comparing data means describing the relationship between two or more sets of figures — which is higher, by how much, and how that relationship changes.

Comparing two data sets is like describing a race between two runners — sometimes one is ahead, sometimes they're neck and neck, and your job is narrating exactly how their positions change relative to each other.

Language for comparing data

ComparisonExample language
One is higher“Sales were significantly higher than profits.”
They are similar“The two figures were roughly similar.”
The gap changes“The gap between them widened/narrowed over time.”
They cross/meet“The two lines intersected in 2015.”

Why this matters to you

Nearly every Task 1 chart involves more than one data set to compare — this comparison language is what actually earns marks for Task Achievement, since simply describing each line separately misses the relationship the examiner is looking for.

🧪 Try it yourself: Imagine two lines on a graph (like your spending versus your saving over a year) and describe their relationship out loud using at least two phrases from the table.

🔑 Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Gap

The difference in size or amount between two data sets

Intersect

To cross or meet at one point

Study tip: Whenever a Task 1 chart shows two or more data sets, always include at least one sentence directly comparing them — this is exactly what separates a strong response from a merely adequate one.

lessons.title: 10.1 Task 1 Vocabulary
lessons.html:
Task 1 VocabularyLesson note
🤔 Let's start with a question
You understand the structure and strategy for Task 1 perfectly. But if you use the word “increase” fifteen times in one essay, how much does that hurt your score?

Task 1 Vocabulary

In plain words

This topic brings together the essential Task 1 vocabulary — trend words, comparison words, and precise numbers — needed to avoid repetition and describe data accurately.

Vocabulary variety in Task 1 is like having several tools instead of just one hammer — using different, precise words for similar ideas (rise, climb, surge) shows the examiner a wider, more skilled vocabulary range.

Building Task 1 vocabulary range

CategoryWord options
Increaserise, climb, grow, surge, soar
Decreasefall, drop, decline, plummet, dip
No changeremain stable, stay constant, plateau
Degreeslightly, significantly, dramatically, marginally

Why this matters to you

Vocabulary range is one of the four criteria IELTS Writing is directly scored on — repeating the same three or four words throughout a Task 1 response noticeably caps this score, however accurate your data description otherwise is.

🧪 Try it yourself: Take one sentence you'd normally write with the word “increase” and rewrite it three different ways using different words from the table above.

🔑 Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Vocabulary range

The variety of different words a writer uses, rather than repeating the same ones

Degree word

A word showing how much or how strongly something changed, like “slightly” or “dramatically”

Study tip: Build your own small personal list of 3-4 alternative words for “increase,” “decrease,” and “stay the same” — reusing this same list across every Task 1 practice builds natural variety fast.

lessons.title: 1.1 Essay Structure
lessons.html:
Essay StructureLesson note
🤔 Let's start with a question
You have strong opinions and good vocabulary. But without a clear structure, will the examiner actually be able to follow your argument?

Essay Structure

In plain words

Essay structure is the standard organisation of a Task 2 essay: an introduction, clear body paragraphs, and a conclusion, each with its own specific job.

Essay structure is like the frame of a building: even the most beautiful materials (your ideas and vocabulary) collapse into confusion without a solid frame holding everything together in the right place.

The standard Task 2 structure

PartPurpose
IntroductionParaphrase the question and state your overall position
Body paragraph 1Your first main idea, explained and supported with an example
Body paragraph 2Your second main idea, explained and supported with an example
ConclusionSummarise your position clearly, without new ideas

Why this matters to you

IELTS examiners specifically score “Coherence and Cohesion,” which rewards a clear, predictable structure — even excellent ideas lose marks if the essay feels disorganised or hard to follow from paragraph to paragraph.

🧪 Try it yourself: Take any essay question you know and write just the four topic sentences (one per part) that would structure your response, without writing the full essay yet.

🔑 Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Introduction

The opening paragraph stating the topic and your position

Conclusion

The final paragraph summarising your overall position

Study tip: Before writing a full essay, always plan your four-part structure first — a few minutes of planning saves you from a confused, hard-to-follow response later.

lessons.title: 2.1 Opinion Essays
lessons.html:
Opinion EssaysLesson note
🤔 Let's start with a question
A question asks “To what extent do you agree or disagree?” Do you actually need to pick just one clear side, or can you sit on the fence?

Opinion Essays

In plain words

An opinion essay asks for your personal view on a statement, and requires you to state and consistently support one clear position throughout.

An opinion essay is like a courtroom lawyer's argument: you pick a clear side and build your entire case around it, rather than presenting both sides equally and leaving the verdict undecided.

Structuring an opinion essay

PartContent
IntroductionState your clear opinion (agree, disagree, or partly agree)
Body paragraph 1Your first reason, with an example
Body paragraph 2Your second reason, with an example
ConclusionRestate your opinion clearly

Why this matters to you

A common mistake is writing an essay that discusses both sides equally without ever stating a clear personal position — opinion essays specifically require you to pick and consistently defend one clear stance throughout.

🧪 Try it yourself: Take an opinion question (like “Should students choose their own subjects?”) and write one sentence clearly stating your position, plus one supporting reason.

🔑 Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Position

The clear stance or opinion you take and defend throughout an essay

Consistent

Staying with the same opinion throughout, without contradicting yourself

Study tip: Decide your position BEFORE you start writing, and write it down clearly in your introduction — this keeps the rest of your essay focused and consistent.

lessons.title: 3.1 Discussion Essays
lessons.html:
Discussion EssaysLesson note
🤔 Let's start with a question
A question asks you to “Discuss both views and give your own opinion.” Is that actually different from a simple agree/disagree essay?

Discussion Essays

In plain words

A discussion essay requires you to fairly present two different views on a topic, before giving your own opinion, usually in the conclusion.

A discussion essay is like a balanced news report followed by an editorial comment — you first present both sides fairly and evenly, then clearly state your own view at the end.

Structuring a discussion essay

PartContent
IntroductionIntroduce the topic and both views, without giving your opinion yet
Body paragraph 1Explain the first view, with a supporting reason
Body paragraph 2Explain the second view, with a supporting reason
ConclusionState your own opinion clearly

Why this matters to you

A common mistake is discussing only one view, or giving your opinion too early — discussion essays specifically require BOTH views to be explained fairly before your own personal opinion appears, usually at the very end.

🧪 Try it yourself: Take a discussion question (like “Some people prefer to work from home, others prefer an office. Discuss both views.”) and write one sentence fairly explaining each side.

🔑 Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Discuss both views

Explaining two different perspectives on a topic fairly, before giving your own

Fairly

Giving equal, balanced attention to each side of an argument

Study tip: Give genuinely equal space and effort to both views before revealing your own opinion — an unbalanced discussion essay loses marks even if your final opinion is well argued.

lessons.title: 4.1 Problem-Solution Essays
lessons.html:
Problem-Solution EssaysLesson note
🤔 Let's start with a question
A question describes a serious problem, like traffic congestion, and asks for solutions. Is naming one solution enough, or do you need more?

Problem-Solution Essays

In plain words

A problem-solution essay requires clearly explaining a problem and then proposing realistic solutions to address it.

This essay type is like a doctor's diagnosis followed by treatment — you first clearly identify what's actually wrong, then propose specific, realistic remedies rather than vague wishes.

Structuring a problem-solution essay

PartContent
IntroductionIntroduce the problem and preview that solutions will follow
Body paragraph 1Explain the problem and its causes or effects clearly
Body paragraph 2Propose one or two realistic solutions
ConclusionSummarise the problem and your proposed solution(s)

Why this matters to you

Vague solutions like “the government should do something” score poorly — strong problem-solution essays propose specific, realistic actions (like “introducing a congestion charge” rather than just “reduce traffic”), which is exactly what raises your Task Achievement score.

🧪 Try it yourself: Take a real problem you know about (like poor internet access in rural areas) and write one specific, realistic solution, not a vague general statement.

🔑 Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Cause

What creates or leads to a problem

Realistic solution

A specific, practical action that could actually address a problem

Study tip: Always make your proposed solution specific and actionable — “build more schools in rural areas” scores far better than a vague “education should be improved.”

lessons.title: 5.1 Advantages & Disadvantages Essays
lessons.html:
Advantages & Disadvantages EssaysLesson note
🤔 Let's start with a question
A question asks you to discuss the advantages and disadvantages of something, like online learning. Do you also need to give your own opinion, or just list both sides?

Advantages & Disadvantages Essays

In plain words

An advantages and disadvantages essay requires you to explain both the benefits and drawbacks of a topic, sometimes also stating which you believe outweighs the other.

This essay is like weighing something on a scale — you place the benefits on one side and the drawbacks on the other, and sometimes state clearly which side you believe is heavier.

Structuring an advantages/disadvantages essay

PartContent
IntroductionIntroduce the topic and preview that both sides will be discussed
Body paragraph 1Explain the advantages, with examples
Body paragraph 2Explain the disadvantages, with examples
ConclusionSummarise, and give your view on which outweighs the other, if asked

Why this matters to you

Always check the exact question wording carefully — some ask only to “discuss the advantages and disadvantages,” while others specifically ask you to say “do the advantages outweigh the disadvantages,” which requires an extra, clear opinion statement.

🧪 Try it yourself: Take a topic like “advantages and disadvantages of social media” and write one clear advantage and one clear disadvantage, each with a brief supporting example.

🔑 Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Advantage

A benefit or positive point about something

Outweigh

To be greater or more important than something else

Study tip: Read the exact question wording twice before starting — “discuss advantages and disadvantages” and “do advantages outweigh disadvantages” require subtly different responses.

lessons.title: 6.1 Two-Part Questions
lessons.html:
Two-Part QuestionsLesson note
🤔 Let's start with a question
A question asks two separate things at once: “Why is this happening, and what can be done about it?” Is it safe to only answer one of them well?

Two-Part Questions

In plain words

A two-part question asks two distinct questions within one essay task, and both parts must be answered clearly and fairly equally.

A two-part question is like being asked two separate exam questions disguised as one — answering only one thoroughly, and ignoring or rushing the other, means you've only half-completed the actual task.

Structuring a two-part question essay

PartContent
IntroductionIntroduce the topic and preview that both questions will be answered
Body paragraph 1Fully answer the first question
Body paragraph 2Fully answer the second question
ConclusionBriefly summarise both answers

Why this matters to you

Missing or under-answering one part of a two-part question directly and significantly damages your Task Achievement score, since the examiner is specifically checking whether BOTH questions were addressed properly, not just one.

🧪 Try it yourself: Find a two-part question (like “Why do some people choose to work abroad, and what are the effects?”) and write one clear sentence directly answering each separate part.

🔑 Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Two-part question

A Task 2 prompt that actually asks two separate questions

Fully answer

Giving a complete, developed response, not just a brief mention

Study tip: Before writing, underline both questions within the prompt — it's an easy way to make sure you don't accidentally miss or rush either one.

lessons.title: 7.1 Linking Words
lessons.html:
Linking WordsLesson note
🤔 Let's start with a question
Your ideas are good individually, but do they actually connect smoothly to each other, or do they feel like a list of separate, disconnected points?

Linking Words

In plain words

Linking words are words and phrases that connect ideas smoothly within and between sentences, showing the reader how your ideas relate to each other.

Linking words are like road signs connecting different parts of a journey — without them, a reader has to guess how one idea leads to the next, rather than being clearly guided along the way.

Common linking words by function

FunctionExamples
Adding an ideaFurthermore, in addition, moreover
ContrastingHowever, on the other hand, whereas
Giving a resultTherefore, as a result, consequently
Giving an exampleFor example, for instance, such as

Why this matters to you

Linking words are directly scored under “Coherence and Cohesion” — but overusing too many complex linking words in a row can actually sound unnatural, so aim for a natural mix rather than cramming in every advanced word you know.

🧪 Try it yourself: Take two separate sentences you've written before and connect them using one linking word from the table above.

🔑 Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Coherence

How logically and clearly ideas connect and flow together

Linking word

A word or phrase connecting ideas, like “however” or “therefore”

Study tip: Use a natural mix of simple and more advanced linking words — a whole essay overloaded with only advanced connectors like “furthermore” can actually sound forced rather than fluent.

lessons.title: 8.1 Cohesion & Coherence
lessons.html:
Cohesion & CoherenceLesson note
🤔 Let's start with a question
Your essay uses linking words correctly and has clear paragraphs. Is that already enough to guarantee a high “Coherence and Cohesion” score?

Cohesion & Coherence

In plain words

Cohesion means how well individual sentences connect together (through linking words and references), while coherence means how logically the whole essay flows as one connected argument.

If cohesion is the glue holding individual bricks together, coherence is the overall shape of the finished wall — you need both the small connections AND a sensible overall structure for the whole thing to genuinely work.

Building cohesion and coherence together

ElementExample
Linking wordsHowever, therefore, for example
Reference words“This issue,” “these factors” referring back to something already mentioned
Logical paragraph orderEach paragraph follows sensibly from the one before
One idea per paragraphAvoids mixing unrelated points together confusingly

Why this matters to you

Cohesion and Coherence is one of the four official IELTS Writing scoring criteria — strong linking words alone (cohesion) aren't enough if the paragraphs themselves are organised illogically (poor coherence); both need to work together.

🧪 Try it yourself: Look at an essay or paragraph you've written before and check: does each paragraph follow logically from the one before it, and do your linking words connect ideas smoothly?

🔑 Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Cohesion

How well sentences connect together, through linking words and references

Coherence

How logically an entire piece of writing flows as one connected argument

Study tip: Read your finished essay from start to finish as if you were a stranger — if the ideas flow logically and nothing feels out of place, your coherence is likely strong.
